THE BURIED MOTHER. Out by the walls of a Danish town It The graves stood cold as the nizht came down. The Angelus prayer had long been said, 7 And the bell tolled out the psalm for the dead; It swung for awhile from the darkening steeple. 61 Out of the depths," said priest and people. Through all the close-set town and towers The doors were shut for the silent hours. But a mother, buried for half a year, Woke with a crying in her ear. She rose with a vague sleep still in her head, And clad in the shroud that wraps the dead. She left the cold graves under the walls, , • And took the,street to her husband's halls. t She felt her long-dead bosom ache, For her seven children were all awake; And none had broken them bread that night, Or poured them milk, or trimmed a light. And none had laid them pillow or sheet, The dust of the day was on their feet. :1;:71 Two strove for an empty cup, and one Was crying—that was her youngest son. She washed and kissed them, and hushed their cries; While tears pressed out of her long-dead eyes, But their father, who lay on a lower floor, Had heard her step in the corridor. And he rose and came, and saw her stand - With the children clinging to either hand. She said "The crying smote my heart. /t broke my dreams of death apart. "I was loth to leave these seven. 1 died. • But when have I slept when the child has cried? "Take note, ere I pass to my many dead: Your children woke and had no bread, "No fire, no lamp; two were at strife; One cried uncomforted. Tell your wi.fe." Aucz Monism. If thou art not able to make thyself that which thou wishest to be, how can'st thou expect to mould another in cotiformity to thy will? "He's not what you call strictly handsome," said the major, beaming through his glasses on an utterly hideous baby, as it lay peacefully howling in its mother's arms; " but its the kind of face that grows on you." "Its not the kind of face that ever grew on you," was the indig- nant and unexpected reply of the maternal being, "you'd be better looking if it had." . When Junius Brutus and the sons of Tarquin asked the Delplic Oracle who was to succeed Superbus on the throne of Rome, the oracle answered," He who shall first kiss his mother" The two princes hastened home to fulfill what they thought was indicated. Brutus, however, fell to the earth and exclaimed, "Thus kiss I thee, 0 earth, thou mother of us all." In all policies of insurance these, among a host of other questions, occur :—" Ago of father, if living?" "Age of mother, if living ?" A man in tha country who filled up an application made his father's age, if living," one hundred and twelve years, and his mother's one hundred and two. The agent was amazed at this, and fancied he had secured an excellent customer; but feeling some- what dubious, he remarked that the applicant came of a very long-lived family. "Oh, you see, sir," replied he, "my parents died many years ago, but if living,' would be aged as there put down." " Exactly—l understand," said the agent. There is a touching story of Lady Rachel Russell, that heroic wife and devoted mother, concealing from a daughter whom she was nursing through a serious ill- ness that one of her sisters had just died of a similar malady. The invalid, who was aware of her sister's illneSs, was full of inquiries about her, which Lady , Russell answered truthfully until the girl's death. The doctors warned her that it might be fatal to the sur- vivor to know this, and the mother took her place in the sick-room with unmoved countenAnce, quieting the 1 invalid with the reply, "Your sister is out of bed to- day," the body having been placed in the coffin. THE ART OF EARLY RISING.—The proper time to rise, says the Lancet, is when sleep ends. Dozing should not be allowed. True sleep is the aggregate of sleep, or is a state consisting in the sleeping or rest of all the several parts of the organism. Sometimes one and at other times another part of the body, as a whole, may be the least fatigued, and so the first to awake, or the most exhausted, and therefore the most difficult to arouse. The secret of good _sleep is, the physiological conditions

After a very few days of self-discipline, the man who resolves not to doze, that is, not to allow some sleepy part of his body to keep him in bed aftertis brain has once awakened, will find himself, without knowing why, an early riser. A certain Jew money-lender, once upon a time (says the Graphic), took the Garrick Theatre, in Leman-street, Whitechapel, and to make a good beginning, opened it I with "Hamlet," a certain popular West End tragedian being engaged to sustain the role. The theatre was in very low repute at the time, even in its immediate neigh- bourhood; and on the opening night he sent forth com- plimentary admissions to all the principal tradespeople around. Now, this tragedian followed the old traditions of the part, and went about in the second act with "his hose ungartered" and hanging down his leg. When Mr. Moses, as we'll call him, caught sight of this from the back of the boxes; he rnshed round behind the scenes, and furiously assailed the prompter. "Vat is the mean- ing of this ?" he cried. "Vat does that man mean by, not tying up his stockings? I never was no ashamed of anything in all my life. There's Mrs. Abrahams, the fruiterer, and Mrs. Jacobs, the fishmonger, and all the elite of the neighbourhood in; it will ruin me." "But it is quite right, sir," said the prompter, showing him the book." Mr. noses put on his spectacles and examined the passage. "Who wrote this play ?" he cried, more wrathfully than ever. "Why, Shakspere, sir," an- swered the astonished functionary. "Then," cried Mr. Moses, shaking his forefinger, "you may tell Mr. Shaks- pere that he'll never write another play for my theatre." Doherty, a former Chief Justice of Ireland, used to tell a good story of his posting days. He was going cir- cuit in a post-chase, and at a dangerous part, where the road skirted a descent, one of the horses, which had been behaving wildly all the way, began kicking furi- ously. Much alarmed, Doherty called out: This is out- rageous. I don't think that horse has ever been in har- ness before." Bedad, your Lordship's right. He was only took out of the field this morning." "And do you mean to tell me that you have put an unbroken horse to my carriage? " Sorra a sight of the leather he has ever seen till to-day. And if he brings your Lordshin safe to the fut of the hill, the master says he'll buy him.' THE MONARCH OF THE NEW FOHEST.—Through the trees one catches a glimpse of the great trunk of the old oak. It is unmistakeable; its size dwarfs all the other trees, even those in its immediate vicinity which are large and well grown. None are quite close to it. These larger trees, which seem to be its companions, form a circle at a respectful distance. It gives an impression as if a monarch were here holding his court. The king is king by right of his strength; the few in the wood- land.who are fit to be his courtiers are near, but not too near; the great tree must have room to breathe, and kills out the others, for he needs all the nourishment of the soil in the empty space around him. Four persons can embrace his trunk with arms outstretched to the full and finger-tips just touching finger-tips. From this huge trunk rise a number of branches, each large enough for an ordinary good-sized tree-trunk; they are flung up to some considerable distance before they are broken by small branches, and the foliage of the tree is all far away overhead.—The English Illustrated Magazine for June. SOCIETY IN LONDON BY ONE OF THE CHOWD.—One afternoon attracted by the singularly-refined face of a flower-girl passing in the Strand, I went up to her, bought some of her flowers, and asked her to come and sit to me, explaining that I wished to "take her like- ness." She said, rather condescendingly:, that as her business-time was chiefly of an evening when the theatres were open, she would consent to do so. The next morning, an hour after the appointed time, my flower-girl appeared. She looked nonchalantly about her; then, seeing a large mirror, stood some time before it in silence, gazing lovingly at herself,.and at length ex- claimed, "Well, it is a rare chance to see oneself like this !" and turned her small antique head from side to side, bridling and peacocking with infinite grace. She was shy, and yet defiant. Her clothes hung closely and yet loosely round her graceful form, showing the deficiency of underclothing. Her head was bare; her beautiful, rusty hair in rich profusion gathered up in a careless knot. When the cold wind blew she drew her ragged shawl over her head. Her ignorance, her knowledge, her audacity were fairly bewildering. She seemed to have no affections no ambitions. Sometimes she would laugh, as if born to do nothing else, but with a melan- choly look in her eyes. This young forsaken thing lived alone in a room she paid for by the week. She liked to stay in bed till ten or eleven in the morning, though on market days it was necessary to be at Covent Garden very early to buy flowers. These she arranged as taste- fully as possible with wire, leaves, and fern, placing them in a light flat basket filled with moss, which is usually car- ried tilted on the palm of the hand. In the afternoon she took up her stand at the entrance to some restaurant in the Strand, or by the approaches to Charing Cross Station. As soon as the theatres opened she hovered about the entrances, but on wet nights no one would linger to buy "button-holes." People only thought of hurrying into or away from the theatres, so the unsold flowers had to be carried home and kept fresh if possible, to be palmed off, when they seemed withered, in dark corners of the street, "not too near the street lamps." The girl could read, she said, but "didn't hold to books." Ladies never gave her anything she cared to read; it was always "goody rubbish they wouldn't so much as look at their- sets." She .used sometimes to attend a sewing-class, where ladies came to read aloud twice a week, "but it was heavy reading." Once an old gentleman "preached" about scarlet fever, and what poor people should do; "but there wasn't much sense in what he said," was her only comment. One of the greatest pleasures she con- fessed was looking in at shop windows—especially the jewellers' shops in the Strand. Lockets, earnings, and bracelets, she spoke of with something like fervour. The photographs of actresses, professional beauties, and the royalties, seemed also a source of unfailing interest. "I don't think much of Mrs. Langtry; I know plenty of girls about the market quite as well-looking, though not so stylish." She much objected to the Queen being photographed in a bonnet and the Prince of Wales in a tall hat. "It ain't distinguished; it don't matter so much how the royal people looks indoors, but they shouldn't go out in them common things."—" The London Ragamuffin,' in The English Illustrated Magazine for June. The loss on the warbid hide is stated by Mr. Hutton to be one penny per pound, and, taking the i statistics of two markets n Birmingham, he showed that the proportion of warbled hides to sound ones in the course of seven weeks was 1,908 of the former to 3,279 of the latter, entailing a deficiency in their sales of 545 pounds, The subject is alluded to in the recently-issued , Journal of the Royal Agricultural Society by. Miss ] Eleanor A.Ormerod, who recommended a dressing of mercurial ointment instead ot piercing the warbled swelling with a knife, which is so frequently done. Mr. T. Duckham, M.P., has given a word of caution as to the employment of any mercurial preparation, as a farmer of Herefordshire, a short time since, by dressing the coats of his cattle with such for the destruction of parasites, killed his animals likewise, through their licking it off with their tongues and introducing ' licking it off with their tongues and introducing the poisonous application into their systems! Mr. Duckham recommends dusting the backs of cattle with sulphur flour as being almost equally efficacious and perfectly harmless. He tried this in his own herd not long since, and only two were found affected with a single warble each afterwards, and these lie readily destroyed -by applying an ointment of carbolic and intermixed with Log's lard in the proportion of 1 to 20 weight. ONE OF THE APPLE TREES' ENEMIES.—MiSS Eleanor Ormerod writes :—" Information has been requested re- garding prevention of attack of codlin moth caterpillar. This does much harm in some years by feeding within the growing apples, until the destruction of the centre of the fruit causes it to fall to the ground. The simple plan of having the small fallen apples (which are quite worthless) gathered up as soon as possible, and destroyed before the caterpillar has left the fruit is the best method of prevention. The caterpillar .usually leaves the apple soon after it has fallen, and crawls up the tree to turn to chrysalis, or in some cases hybernate in caterpillar state under rough bark or other shelter. If, therefore, the grubs can be prevented crawling up the stem by a band of any stick composition being smeared round the low 6 part of the trunk, much of this attack would be pre- vented. For present prevention (even as late as the nest week or two) it would be worth while, in the case of choice trees which are suspected of being infested, to scrape off any rough bark, and rub and brush soft soap well into any forks or rifts where the chrysalids, or even hybernated caterpillars, may be sheltering. It has been found in Germany and in California, though I am not aware that it has been reported in England, that the caterpillar sometimes winters beneath the surface of the earth, close to the trunk of the tree, or in decayed roots. I therefore advise turning the soil back, just round the stem, to a depth of about six inches, and replacing it with a little fresh soil and quicklime. In my own garden I have had the ground, for about a foot round all the trees, soaked on the surface with paraffin and water." DIaTRICT AGRICULTURAL NOTES.—A correspondent writes :—The change in the weather has been of invalu- able service to almost every form of crop in this dis- trict. The rain has been copious, but it can hardly be considered ample in most •places, and certainly not on some of the drier soils. The temperature has improved, and, combined with the increased moisture, has made a great change in the appearance of the country. More uniform warmth is still, however, much wanted. At times the winds are bitter and chop about from one point of the compass to the other, and the colder fits undo the good done by the m6re kindly breezes. Grass has made a great push on the better soils, but generally speaking it is by no means satisfactory as regards quan- tity, either on pasture or meadows. Many pastures are painfully bare. In the country lying between Preston and Lancaster, between the coast and the fells, there is a positive scarcity of grass. There were loud complaints amongst the farmers; on the fell side there was not only a scarcity of grass, but all the hay Was done. The colds appear to have told more in that district than in the country between Manchester and Liverpool, and yet in this part there is no great quantity of grass. Oats have pulled up nicely in a good many places, and have greatly benefited by the rain, but it is to be feared that the com- bined influences of cold, drought, grub, and wireworm have left traces behind them which cannot be recovered. This is certainly the case in many poor fields that.l have seen, and especially is it true of stiff clay soils, where the ground is exhausted and there is nothing added in the way of manure to fortify the sickly plant. I met with many instances of this kind between Manchester and Galgate. A fortnight's fine weather will alter the appearance of oats very much. The ketlock has ap- peared in the more forward oats. Wheat has improved in colour and strength, and that sickly yellow which was beginning to appear on poorer land has been replaced by blades of a more healthy hue. Potato seed is all in, and a great quantity has been planted all over Lanca- shire and Cheshire. BATHING HORSES.—Our own health cannot be assured if bathing is neglected. The skin must be kept free of impediments to the full discharge of its office. Now, this is true also of the animal. It is a little strange that water is not more frequently used upon our stock. The pores of their skin become clogged, and there is a scurf upon them which causes discomfort. Cattle and swine rub, horses roll as soon as given an opportunity, and indicates, if there is no skin disease, that there is more or less irritation from the iccurnulations on the surface. A thorough bathing would remove these, and greatly, add to the comfort of the animal. The horse, especially, is liable to have this kind of irritation. He sweats pro- fusely, and this, with the dust and dirt that settles upon the animal, works into the pores, and stops there, and forms a sort of crust upon the surface. The curry comb will not wholly remove it, for it cannot reach all of it. But a good bath will Largely remove it. We observe that the practice of giving the horse a Turkish bath in case of sickness has been introduced, and we regard it as a very excellent thing. • Most of our readers doubtless understand what a Turkish bath is. It is in part a pro- cess of sweating by which the obstructions in the pores of the skin are removed. A human being may wash himself until he believes himself to be perfeetly clean, but a Turkish bath immediately afterwaids will cause the dirt to fairly roll off him. The obstructions in the pores are reached. Of course, the Turkish bath can be administered only in apartments constructed for that purpose. It requires rooms with a very high degree of heat, and those with a less degree, facilities for cold bath- ing, &c. But the common bath, or common washing, is in the direction of producing the same results. It softens to some degree the hardened matter that has entered the pores, and lies over the pores, and thus permits a freer egress for the worn-out particles of the system that escape through the skin. Animals greatly enjoy the pro- cess of washing or bathing, as anyone who has ever per- mitted them to enjoy the luxury can testify. The same precaution should be taken as we take with reference to bathing ourselves. The processes should be precisely similar, so far as it is possible. It should not be done when the animal is in a perspiration, and we should not do it immediately after meals. The animal should be rubbed perfectly dry, and it is not advisable to bathe in

during the day, or- from six4ill .six, seemed to•alarm them and keep them fairly away. But as they: were busy between those hours, we placed a herring net:over the seed bed. Many, however, managed to gel under the net and were captured, an odd one occasionally escaping. Now we never see one. Probably those that escaped were the ringleaders, and the warning they have received has been salutary in deterring them from lead- ing their fellow-marauders into our premises so long as the net is in sight. THE FRONT GARDEN.—Chrysanthemums, if they have not been propagated by cuttings, may have the old roots divided into pieces with two or three shoots each, which may either be planted where they are intended to flower, or potted and kept in a shady comer for a few days if intended for the window. Bulbous plants as they go out ()flower should have their position indicated by some imperishable material, such as pieces of wira the thickness of an ordinary lead pencil, thrust into the ground a foot deep, er narrow strips of iron painted white on the upper six inches, and the name of the bulb written on with a pencil before it dries will do equally well; and add to the interest of the garden. The grass plot should be closely mown, especially now there is so much traffic on it during the operation of planting. Grass left to get unduly long gives. much more trouble to cut.

I Only once did she hear his name in the two years that I followed, and that was in connection with the scheme of some proposed Government works, and he was called Mr. Fellowes, the well-known and using engineer." Dick rising! Dick fatuous! Stella was sensible of a little shock of intense wonder. But there was very little time for any thought of the !Outside world after that. Colonel Howard died in Afghani- , !Stan, and Stella found herself a penniless orphan, dependent on the distant relatiene with whom she was living. Even in all her sone* and despair there was a little ray of comfort In the thought of Captain Thurlow. Surely there was one strong arm and brave heart that would not fail her. But Captain Thurlow was endowed with a knowledge of the world, which made him keenly aware of the nice difference betweea Miss Howard the pretty daughter of his reputedly wealthy colonel, and Miss Howard the penniless orphan. His engagement to a Lancashire manufacturer's daughter was in all the society papers within a fortnight ; and as Stella tried to crush out the mortification and resentment from her heart, which seemed full to overflowing, there sounded in her ears, as if it were a prophecy, Dick Fellowes' parting words, "No one will ever love you as I have done." Was it all the perversity of a woman's nature that made Sheila's memory dwell so often and so kindly on the memory of that wooing as time.went on? In the old days life had held so much love for her that Dick's seemed a thing little worth the having; new that she was that lonely thing, a go'verneessin other people's Noises, she wondered how she could have despised any love so honest and so Doi& and her recollection of clumsy Dick grew to be a very kind and gentle one. Not that her lot was as hard as mane; indeed, the Bonchers were very kind to her. Her pupils were good and affectionate, with the careless affection of children; she bad plenty to eat and drink,- and nothing to complain of, except that life had passed her by. She tried to do her duty, to teach the children well and wisely, to help Mrs. Boucher with her many guests and society cares. The house was to be full for regatta week, as usual, and Stella had promised to give up her holiday till after they were all alone again. .She was writing- notes for a great garden- party, when the little girls burstin upon her in wild excite- ment. " Oh, Miss Howard! only think!" they cried—" Sir Riohie sin coming—our, own dear Sir Richie! Isn't it lovely ?" and they gambolled about her like frisky kittens. "And who may Sir Richie be ?" inquired Miss Howard composedly, directing her envelope& "Not know oar, Sir Richie? Why, everybody knows him! He plays tennis with us, and rows us on the lake, and buys us dolls ! . Fancy, mamma! Miss Howard doesn't know our darling Richie P ' "Miss Howard hae been out of society for so long," re- sponded Mrs. Boucher, more sedately, "that there is an ex- cuse for her not knowing at least the name of Sir Richard Fellowes." The pen rolled on the newly-addressed envelopes, and ruined two. "Sir Richard Fellowes!" was all Miss Howard could gasp out. " Yes, the great inventor and civil engineer. He had his baronetcy conferred a few months ago, when he finished the great railway line to Thibet ; and he's just been stopping at Osborne. Is it possible you've never heard his name? Why, he was one of the lions of last season—young, rich, and the fashion. I'm lucky to get him here even for a flying visit; but my husband and he are old friends, and he's wonderfully fond of the chicks. Can you never have heard of him, really ?" " I—l met him years ago, I remember,' Stella just man- aged to falter. "Then people would think you fortunate. However, I fear you won't have much chance to renew your old ac- quaintance: Sir Richie, as the childfen call him, is such an object of attention from both clibutantes and chaperones. He's one of the great partis of the year." And Mrs. Boucher laughed a little good-natured laugh. Gladly—gladly would Stella have _ hidden herself away in her distant schoolroom that night, and pleaded neuralgia, or any other synonym for an aching heart, rather than enter the crowded drawing-room, whence the soft flow of voices and laughter floated out from the open windows ever to her own room in the wing. But Mrs. Boucher had told her they would want souse singing, and governesses must not indulge their feelings when other people's entertainment is at stake. Stella's heart seemed beating in her ears 38 she entered the great drawing- room behind a tray of coffee-cups, and hid herself in a shel- tered corner noir the piano. At first she could see nothing clearly, the rose-shaded lamps threw so dim a light; then she grew aware of a group of smiling, interested people, all bestowing their most gra- cious smiles and attention on a tall figure in their midst. Could that be Dick Fellowes—that broad-shonldereci man, with the long brown moustache and close-cropped curly head, who moved and looked and spoke like amen easily con- fident of his own powers, and used to succeed and please? Stella thought of the ill-fitting garments of old days as she noticed the shapely out of his coat-collar and the grace of self-possession in Sir Richard Richie's every movement. Dick had red anls and big boots, and suggested a bull in a china-shop. Was there some mistake, after all ? A moment, and then he raise]. his head, and she caught the old merry smile and the flash of the quick grey eyes; and, half blinded and bewildered with the rush of recollection, Stella made her way to the piano, in obedience to Mrs. Boucher's nod and smile. Why had Mrs. Boucher asked her to sing "ffoldea Days?" It was Dick's favourite song long ago, and Stella felt as if it would choke her. Her voice shook so that Mrs. Boucher's guests thought their hostess had 'a good deal over-praised her governess's style, and a Miss Verney near by remarked to Sir Richard Fellowes that she did not admire that tremolo kind of manner so many girls affected. Ah, for the days beyond recalling Ah, for the golden days! sang Stella, with something that was like a sob—so like, that she pulled herself up sharply, and felt as if she had fallen for ever in hei own respect. As she rose from the piano-stool, her eyes met those of Sir Richie standing close to her side. There was nothing beyond the most casual recognition in the slight bow on both sides, and then Stella got away somehow to her own quarters, to find vent for the passionate flow of tears which overcame all her self-control. Next day was to be the grand garden-party. Miss Howard was supposed to be unostentatiously in the background, dressed in her best, to keep a supervision over her little pupils. Ethel and Maudie, wild with delight, hastened her out to•the tennis-lawn long before any one could possibly be expected to arrive. "Just one little game before people come, to try the ground, Miss Howard," they begged. "You know we mayn't play when all the grown-ups are here, and we do so want a little tiny game." Miss Howard, mindful of her beet- cream gown, and the difficulties of tennis when combined with a plumed hat and long gloves, vainly endeavoured to escape. ' Only a little scrap of play," they said. "Ah Iyon know you can't refuse," And Stella was forced to (I laugh and yiele,

Beatrie.—The following anecdote of a famous French- woman proves the truth of the old saying, "Handsome is that handsome does." A famous lady who once reigned hi Paris society was so homely that her mother said one day, "My poor child, you are too ugly for any one ever to fall in love with you." From this time Madame de Cireourt began to be very kind to the pauper children of tile village, the servants of the household, even the birds that hopped about the garden walks. She was always distressed if she happened to be unable to render a service. This good will toward everybody made her the idol of the city. Though her complexion was sallow, her gray eves small and sunken„yet she held in devotion to her the greatest men of her time. Her unfailing interest in others made her, it is said, perfectly irresistible. Her life furnishes us a most valuable lesson. A DINER'S Goon FORTUNE.—The. old divers are fond of recounting the glories of their craft, and are specially impressed with any information as to the fate of the vessels of the Armada. This spirit has been fostered no less by the sticcesses of the ancestor of the Mulgravea than by the good fortune of John Gann, of Whitstable. The old diver was, many years since, employed on the Galway coast, and used to pass his evenings in a public. house frequented"by fishermen. One of these men, re- peating a tradition which had long existed in the dis- trict, told Gann that one of the Spanish vessels had been wrecked not far from that coast, and intimated that he himself could point out the spot. Gann, having finished his special job, made terms with the fisherman, and they were both out for many weeks dragging the spot indi- cated for any traces of the wreck. They were at last rewarded by coming upon obstructions with their grap- nels. Gann brought out his diving apparatus, and sure enough the truth of the tradition was vindicated by the finding of a number of dollars,which had originally been packed in barrels. The barrels, however, had rotted away, and left the gold stacked in barrel shape. With the money so recovered John Gann built at Whitstable, his native place, a row-of houses, which, to commemo- rate the circumstance, he called Dollar-row. From 44 The Sea," for June, How TO DEAL WITH HAY ASTIIEA.—I cannot help believing that, as in the case of "winter cough," one attack of hay asthma leaves the sufferer more subject to another, still that is no reason why he should not make a bravo stand, even after he has had several, to obtain not only present relief, but future immunity; and, thirdly, in the very fact that some attacks are more severe than others lies hope to the sufferer, for it should lead him to study well the apparent causes of each and to avoid them. Ile may be able to say to himself, "That lmt attack of mine was terribly severe, but then I have to remember that my health at the time it commenced was certainly a little below par." Well, here is one step in advance already, and the hint which I shall now put in words is implied in what I have already written. It is this: People subject to hay asthma cannot be too care- ful in keeping up their health-status. No need for me to tell them how to do this; they must, 'while carefully avoiding, as far as possible, well-known exciting causes, Itive by rule. Here is another hint: While living by rule, t'ley must avoid, in the intervals of their illness, taking ramy drugs. If one does really and truly live by rule, medicine of any kind is hardly. if ever, reqUired. This is all I, or probably any one, can say about constitutional or preventive treatment; there is no prophylactic for hay asthma, that must be apparent to every one.— Cassell's Family Magazine. "Srarra WONDER."—This famous grotto—Fingal's Cave—was visited for the first time in 1722 by Sir Joseph Banks. It is two hundred and twenty-seven feet long, lofty-two feet wide, sixty-six feet high,and at ebb has twenty-five feet of water. On its west ;side the pilLys are thirty-six feet high, those on the east being eighteen feet. From mouth to end the cede is penetrated by a pavement of broken basalt pillars—" fitting together," as Miss Gordon Cumming says, "in faultless honey- comb." It is impossible to describe the cave so as to convey an adequate idea of its grandeur, its beauty, and its entire and strange newness to those who have not seen it. The play of colour is most exquisite, the basalt combining every tint of warm red, brown, and rich maroon; seasveeds and lichens touch it with green and gold; while the lime which has filtered through has crusted the pillars here and there a pure snow-white. From the sombre roof of smooth rock or broken pillars hang yellow, crimson, and white stalactites. The floor of the cave is the green sea, out of which columns rise on either side with a regularity so unbroken as to sug- gest the hand of man rather than the work of Nature. Looking outwards from the interior, the scene is won- derful as the sunlight tips the Atlantic waves, which come surging in with steady swing, and break, with full resounding boom, in the depths of the cavern. Huge tidal wave; roll into the cave at times, and carry every- thing before them. Only once, however, have they caused disaster. In 1884 such a wave swept in as a few Persons were exploring the cave, and one of the party lost his life. Miss Gordon Cumming says that a relation ' of hers narrowly escaped a like fate. On this occasion a mighty wave seemed to fill the whole of the cave's mouth, and he had just time to clasp a pillar, which, fortunately for him, he had noticed to stand detached from its fellows. While the wave boiled and surged. over his head, he clasped the column with the grip of a vice, and saved himself. But for the detached pillar and his happening to notice it, he would assuredly have been swept away. The great tidal wave is a feature of this sea, and one for which the wary are always on the watch.—" Little Folks" for June. FSTABLISHEI) IYEA,:LY tro YEARS. There are two varieties of pencilled Hamburgs, namely, the Gold and Silver Pencilled. The difference between 'these two is entirely that la colour. In the Golds, the ground colour is a yellowish, or deep reddish, bay, with all the feathers, save those on the neck and saddle hackle, which are entirely self-colour, pencilled with several clearly defined bars of black. In the Silver- Pencilled, the ground colour is of a silver white, with the same markings as in the Golds. The distinction, therefore, between the two is that of ground colour alone. These varieties have had many names, and in a work published upwards of forty years ago, just after the name Hamburgh had been given to the breeds, we find the following. The Pencilled Hamburehs are known also as the Bolton Greys (silvers) and the Bolton Bays (golds). "from being extensively and superiorly cultivated in and about Bolton, in Lancashire; Creole (Creel is only a provincial mode of pronouncing Creole), from the inter- mixturdof the black and white; Coral, because the numerous points of the bright-polished, scarlet rose- comb bear no distant resemblance to grains of red coral; Pencilled Dutch, because many are imported from Holland; Dutch Every-day-layers, and Everlastings for the same reason, and their great productiveness as layers ; and Chitteprat, the derivation of which is not so obvious. Chitteface, according to Bailey the lexico- grapher, means a meagre child; and Chitteprat, if intended to describe a diminutive hen, would not be misapplied to one of this variety:, amictA34=.l We do not think that there is any breed which can excel the Pencilled Hamburgh, whether of the golden or silver variety, as pets, or on a lawn where beauty combined with graceful movement is thought desirable. Both sexes are characterised by a neatness and compactness which are specially their own. Iri Wingfield and John- son's Poultry Book, published in 1843, a description of these birds is given, which shows that the same type then existed as now. It says that the cock has a full bright red rose comb, about three-quarters of an inch wide, erect, though low on the head, and regularly pointed, but terminated in a single point or "pike" be- hind, which should extend far back and curve gently upwards; ear lobes, large and white; wattles, large, round, and red; head, small and fine; beak, short and white; plumage, entirely white in the silvers, and bay in the golds, with the exception of the wings and tail; the wings barred very regularly with black; tail ample, very erect, measuring nine inches to the top of the highest curve of the sickle feathers, which are of un- usual length, and with the rest of the tail feathers of a lightly iridescent black, their edges only being verylightly margined with which in the silVers, and bay in the golds. The height may be placed at sixteen inches, while an average weight would reach to 4i pounds. The hen displays the peculiarities which characterise this sub-variety much more distinctly than the cock. The ground colour must be either creamy white or cop- pery-yellow (silver-white or golden-bay is a better de- scription now) accordingly as the birds belong to the silver or golden classes, and each feather marked in either with at least four parallel transverse dark bars, as if an artist had worked them in with a, black lead pencil. Their hen's head is very small and fine; the comb double rose, shaped like that of the cock, but very much smaller; ear-lobes white; eyes in both sexes large and prominent; neck hackle creamy (silver) white or bay, without a black feather; the rest of the plumage, even to the tips of the tail feathers, regularly pencilled throughout; the tail feathers often have a broad black tip; the legs and feet are blue and perfectly clean or featherless; under the belly is often self-colour; but the less of this the better. Spangled feathers mixed with the pencilled are very objectionable, as is also that con- fusion of colouring or sprinkling of black amongst the white, which we should suspect first obtained such Specimens the designation of the Silver Moss Fowl. The weight of the hen is about 31b., and the height about 15_ !inches.

Many of our readers who keep pencilled Hamburghs Will welcome the following hints on the selection of stock birds, written some years ago by our townsman, Mr. Richard Teebay, of Fulwood, than whom there is no better judge. Mr. Teebay wrote Some strains of pencilled Hamburghs occasionally breed hen-tailed cocks that are pencilled like the pullets; these when correctly marked are preferred by some to breed from, as it is genurally thought they breed the best pullets. These hen-feathered cocks are of no use as exhibition birds, neither can they be depended upon for breeding cock- erels for that purpose, as very few of the cockerels bred from them are sufficiently pure in the colour to be ex- hibited with success. For breeding purposes it is far better to choose a cockerel in his chicken feathers, just before he begins to change to the adult plumage; at that time the cockerels are pencilled much the same as the pullets, and one should be selected as perfect as pos- sible in comb and deaf ears, well pencilled with solid black pencilling, the markings equal in width, running straight across the feather, and the width of the pencil- lings not less than the width of the white space be- twixt. If obliged to choose a stock bird in his adult plumage for breeding purposes, he ought to have a sufficient depth of colour in the bottom of his feathers, be quite black on the inside web of his flight feathers, with secondaries pencilled across the inside web with very broad black pencilling, and heavily pencilled across the inside web of his greater wing coverts. His tail should be quite black, and the sickle and curved side feathers should not be more silvered than is required in a bird for exhibition. The greatest care should also be taken to examine the quality of the pencilling in the hens of the same strain. A cock with distinct bars on

" Oh, Sir Richie!' shrieked the children ; " you're jest in time ! Come along, and have a game with Miss Howard —do, do." • Stella turned with a violent start; the racquet slipped from her gloved hand, and struck her left wrist a violent blow. The pain turned her faint and giddy, and she felt herself grow white to her very lips. "No, no, young women," she heard the voice that was so like, vet so unlike the voice of old days say—" Miss Howard won't play with me—she never would." Then, with a sudden change from the laughing tone— "Have you hurt your arm? I'm afraid I startled you ; " and he came forward hastily. But Stella drew away as he approached. "Nothing—it's nothing," she said, almost crossly. "Pray don't trouble; and, as a stream of gaily-dressed people emerged .from the conservatory door, and began to spread themselves over the terrace and approach the lawn, Stella actually tamed and fled into the shrubbery. She had reached the fountain by the statue of the dancing faun before she was overtaken. " Pardon me," said her pursuer, in a tone that was cer- tainly not Dick's—it was too commanding. "I don't want to contradict you, but I can't quite believe it is nothing; and in another moment the little bruised wrist, from which she had stripped the glove, was in Sir Richie's firm, light grasp, and Stella meekly surrendered.

"Sit down here," was the the next order; and she found herself placed on the mossy step of the ruined fountain, ! while, with quick, deft fingers, Sir Richie dipped his hand- kerchief in the cool, clear water, and bound it round the slender wrist. Could it be Dick? Wasn't it all a mocking dream? Stella could only hope with all her might that the awakm.- lug might be long delayed. The splash of the water in the old stone basin, and the , mysterious whisper of the pines overhead, were the only sounds that broke the stillness. The tennis lawn was too far off for them to hear the merry players; they were quite alone. Did Dick remember the last time they had been alone together? He came and sat down on the broken step by her si Is. "Stella," he said, low and gravely, "do you shrink from me still? After all the years that ehave been working and toiling to be worthier of you, am I no nearer the goal than when we last parted? Must I ask in vain, as I did then, for the very least little kind word?" Not a movement, not a sound, from the shrinking figure at his side. His face grew graver still, and he bit his lip. "Am Ito go away again, then?" he asked. Still no answer. With a sudden impulse Sir Richie stooped and peered under the shady hat which hid her face from him.

" What ! crying, Stella!" He was on his knees beside her on the green moss. "Have I made you cry? My darling! my own—" He was trying to take her in his arms, but she struggled to free herself. " Ah, Dick !" she murmured brokenly, "I told you once our lives were poles apart: it was false then, but it has come true." "If it had, which I deny," he said, "the relative posi- tions would be the same. Y6ti are, as you have always been, a world above me in all things. But love can bridge any gulf, Stella: won't you let me try? It's my trade, you know." And then she struggled no longer. "Dick," she whispered, by-and-by, when conversa- tion hld had time to become a trifle less absorbing, "do you remember what you said that night at Churlstone ? You told me no man would ever love me as you had done. I didn't believe it then, but I know you were right now.' "Did I say that ?" he asked, laughing. " Well, yes; I was right, I dare say—only I put it in the wrong tense. What I should have said was, not as I have done,' but as I do, and as I shall ever keep on doing as long as the world shall last.' And that would have been truer still, my guiding star; so let it stand like that for the fatale " • And that point was settled, once and for always.—From Cassell's Magazine" for June.

div.head: DINNER FOR NOWT.
div.p: A DINNER FOR NOWT.

BY AB• 09111.-YATE. I've seen a good deeal i'th' newspappers lately about penny dinners for childer ; an' I believe they con be had, as atin' stuff is now selling'. I've seen an' tasted dinners, an' had to be satisfied wi' my share, seen, year sin', ut had- no' cost a penny a yead. A quartern o' bacon for four on us, three pound o' potatoes, finished th' meal. An' it did- no' last long. Thor nob'dy stood at back o'th' chtears wi' a white napkin on his arm, an' ready fort' tak th' plates away afore they'n empty. He'd ha' had to ha' throttled some- b'dy off 112 fast. Ther nobbut a quarter of an hour gan US to get through th' jab; an' we could ha' spared summat out o' that if there'd bin a jackass, or a strange dog about. Thl.r no weal:tin-up wanted. Th' plates wur as dealt' as when they'rn browt on th' table. Bat there'd bin about four Inches o' window leather, ut's sometimes used for talkin with, gooin' round th' plates like little mops, so that nowt war lost, nor wasted.

Now we con have a dinner for nowt, an' sometimes a glass o' ale thrown in. I couldno' ha' believed it if I hadno' seen it. But Pre down i' Manchester th' tother day, an'happened to co a-talein' my owd friend "Shoiny Jim," at his "Town House" P Timber-street; an' as he hadno' laid in a stock o' atables an' drinkables, no moore than th' family would want, be axt me to dine Wi' him at his hotel—th' "lied. Grunter," Hurdy-gurdy Place, wheere we could have a dinner—a "swell" dinner, for" nothin,' wi' change out." Han they to break stones for it ?" I axt him. "Why, you don't think I'm taking you to the workhouse, do you ?" Jim said, wi' o' his frills out. "Not exactly," I said; but it looks so queer bavin' dinner for nowt that I thowt we must do summat for it. Han we to stond on a stage while we're atin ?" "What do you mean?'

"Well, th' only time I'd ever a dinner at th' same price war when Pre a lad. An' it wur on a mountebank stage upo' Hazalwo'th Green. We'd a traycle cake apiece, hung in a bant, an' we had to ate 'em Wl' our bonds teed beheend 111. That ut geet through th' lust had thrippence for a prize. Little Jammie won. He said he'd had mony a good hoidin in his time, but that war th' best fickin ever he'd had. Shoiny wur disgusted, an' said he'd a good mind to have a cab, fort' show me it war no common place at he're takkin me to. But th' cab didno' turn up. Well, we went to th Red Grunter, an' I fund it war as Jim said, no common sort of a place, as we entered by a gateway, tho' th' gates had bin carried away by Oliver Crummell, an' made to do duty at th' owd Church. There wurno mony folk in at th' time, as we'rn rayther soon ; but Jim said, lookin' at someb'dy else's watch, that we'd a "nice margin. "What's it going to ha ?" a very nice sort of a chap said, th' owner o'th' watch.

"Too late for champagne. I'll take a bitter," Jim said. "What is your friend taking?" "Oh, rit ha' th' same," I said. "That's the Bret course," Jim said. "We take it in- stead of soup. The next will be more substantial. There goes the Eackange clock—eleven. Look out." I looked out, an' thowt ther a thunner-storm cousin' on' th' place went so dark o at once: but I soon fund out it wur a cloud o' folk ut had caused th' darkness. In they coome, one at th' top of another, as if there'd bin a bear outside, lookin out for a bit o' territory. "Watch the attack," Jim said, rowling up his sleeves as if he meant bein' i'th' front, "Thou mun follow me if thou meeans havin' a buster." An' he shuffled a lot o' plates as if he're shufflin' cards. Then ther a big dish coome in wi' a steearn risin' fro' it like a cloud. "Dive in, Ab, or else thou'll get nowt. There's two comin' a second time already."

I di;•ed in an scanded myser th' fast go to. Bat I'd no chance o' gooin a second time; th' dish war empty. But ther another followed. Th' second dish had a very short life; an' then th' crowd began o' gettin' thinner. " Wheere are they o flown to ? " I oat Jim, as th' place went cooler.

"The next shop," Jim said. "They'll be to late to make up a good dinner if they are not off at once. Some'll manage three places; but these are light weights, and can get over tie' ground quick. Astonishing, isn't ic ? "Au' dost' meean to say ut this dinner's gan for nowt every day ? " I said..

"Every day this thing goes on. It used to extend no further than a nibble of bread and cheese. Then a little bacon was put on; then hotpot; but as other hotels were doing it this must follow suit." " Butsome on 'em han had no drink yet," I said. "They've had no time," Jim said. "Lunch fast an' , drink after. Somali dodge the landlord's eye, and if they see they're being watched, they'll get hold of a friend's glass, as/if by mistake. But these you'll find hangin' about the corner outside. They're not customers." "Yigb, but customers o'th' wrong sort, I reckon." "That's about it. Now see how I can work the oracle," an' Jim geet up fro' his seeat. "I'll go out at one door, and come In again at the other." Then he bowted like someb'dy ut had paid for glasses round for o th' company. In another minit or two Jim comes marchin' in at th' front door, looks round as if he're seechin someb'dy •, finds him, an' drops down i'th' next seest, then beckons o'th' bar- maid. I con see he's havin' another glass. He gets it, but doesno' pay for it. Th' tother mon has to fork out. Then he goes at th' bread and cheese, as if he'd never tasted nowt before. After this bit o' pantomime he comes to me. He gets a pipe, an' begs a bit o"bacco, an' looks as comfortable o'er smooking it as if he'd bin givin a lot away. Then he turns to me, an' says— " What do you think of this grand institution, old fellow?"

"Well, I'd rayther be a customer than th' landlord," I said. "How long would this last at th' Owd Bell ?" " Look at the difference in the price of beer," Jim said " Here you pay twopence for mild, and at the old Bell you get it for a penny. See?" Ay, I see. Bat it doesno' cover th' coat o' thy dinner. Thou's had sixpennoth o' lunch an' five pennoth o' ale for nowt. If they wur to charge hauve-a-crown a glass it wouldno' pay." "Right you are, my boy. I've only been showing you how the thing can be done. Thia lunch is put on the table for gentlemen. It is expeciel that none but gentlemen will

TONQUIN EXPEDITION. PARIS, TIJESDAY.—A telegram received here from Lent- sin, of to day's date, anneunceq that a fresh Imperial decree has been issued, ordering Lie Yinh Phuoc, the commander of the Black Flags, to leave Tunquini and directing that the evacuation of Tonquin is to be completed. THE PROPOSED IMPEACHMENT OF TUE FERRY MINISTRY. • PARIS, THURSDAY—The Chamber of Deputies to-day discussed the report of the Committee of Initiative recom- mending the rejection of the motion for the impeachment of the lats Ferry Ministry. M. Brisson, on behalf if the Government, called upon the House to adopt the conclusions of the report. The Premier pointed out the uselessness on the eve of the general election of re-opening a discussion which divided the Republican party, and counselled the Chamber to shorten barren debates. At the conclusion of M. Brisson's speech, which was received with prolonged sp. planse from the Centre, M Riviere ascended the tribune and delivered a speech supeorting the impeachment. LORD ROSEBERY'S VISIT TO BERLIN. BERLIN, SATURDAY.—The semi-official North German Gazdte to-day characterises as imaginary the report of the conversation between Lord Roseberry and the German Chancellor forwarded to a London newspaper by its Paris correspondent, and :it goes on to observe that the object of the communication referred to was evidently no other than to renaw old attempts to stir up stife between England and Germany. It is obvious that all that has been pub- lished as to the subject of conversations at which no wit- nesses were present can rest solely on conjecture. THE SANITARY CONFERENCE. Roust Scaunoay.—The Sanitary Conference has de- cided that the vessels coming from India, on board of wlo:,oh cases of cholera have appeared, should be subject five days' cprarantlne in the Red Sea ports. As a means of disinfection, the Conference gives prekcence to phenic acid.

THE REBELLION IN CANADA. OTTAWA, SUNDAT.—thneral. 'Middleton reports to the Militia Department that he left Battleford to-day for Fort Pitt, in steamers, with three tegiruents of infantry, two Getting guns, and a body of cavalry, to reinforce General Strange, the latter, with 300 men, having been keeping at bay for three days Big Bear and 500 braves, who have been used to Indian warfare, In the United Stetes Big Bear has a stronghold twelve miles north-east of Fort Pitt, in a Country abounding in deep ravines and wild streams, and covered with dense forest. On Thursday General Strange had on fight, which lasted four hours, with Big Bear's force, when the field guns silenced the Indian fire ; but fighting of the same nature Wee resumed the same day. PHILADELPHIA, FRIDAY,—InSpeCIOr Peters, with 20 of the Meented Police, arrived at Battleford to-day from Gene- ral Strange'e column, which has reached Fort Pitt. They bring accounts of some terrible atrocities committed by Big Bear's Indians. The body of a policeman named Cann was foutsd dreadfully mutilated, the heart being cut out and freed on a pole. Six other mutilated and burned corpes were discovered, two being those of priests, and there is evi- dence that tortures were inflicted on the prisoners before they were killed. EARTHQUAKE IN INDIA.—CAVALRY BARRACKS DES nitOYED.—SERIOUS LOSS OF LIFE. BOMBAY, Teesaay.—A telegraphic-desPatch received here announces that a fearful earthquake has devattated a portion of the province of Cashmere, in Northern India. The first shocks were experienced on Sunday, and created intense consternation. The oscillation was repeated at in- tervals of aboeteen minutes, and the shocks still .-continued up to the tirneebis despatch was sent off. Those who were able to control their fears at the first terrestial disturbance were tenable to preserve their presence of mind when the continually-recurring shocks threatened death and destruc- tion to all around. A wild panic eeized npeta the people, who ran to the rivers and lakes, sad sought to escape by , embarking .upon fleeting cr rft of any descKption. Many others have hareily erected tents,arad other .I,ight structures. in the 'open spaces, in which they ,havc sought shelter. SaVeral ',Visitors had already arrivod in the d'.strict for a stay during the hot season. It is irilieved many of these have succumbed, but to what extent teat present unknown. The town eel Srinagar seems to have ruff:seed most severely, according to the information already teeceived. A great portior, of the city has been totally demolished by the most ' severe shocks. The cavalry barracks rt • this station have; 'been' totally destroyed, with many of the inmates. No I fewer than 50 persons were edited emtright in Srinagar, and aevery much larger number have 'been injured by the fall- ing-walls. It is feared, when the facts become fully known, that the death-rAI Wi.ii prove to be very much hi&ser. The distress among themoorer nittives will be very great, And help will be urgently needed. The loss of cattle seems -to have been out of all proportion to what is usually re- corded at such visitations. Sereral hundred beasts haveteen 'destroyed. WEDNESDA.V..—The ,'British Consul resident in Cashmere officially reports that the first shock of earth- "Tuake was felt at Srinagar at three o'clock on Sunday morning. The shotek3continaed en Monday morning, and 'several houses weredestroyede but the toes of life is believed to-be comparatively -small. • The records and furniture of the British Residency hava been removed to tents cc a pre- cautionary measure. SIMLA, WEDNEIDAY,'"X4O•,e.re.—A later despatch from the British Resident in Cashmere states that no Europeans were. killed during the recent earthquake shocks. THE CHOLERA IN SPAIN.

MADRID, WEENESDAY. - The Medical Commission re- cently sent to the province of Valencia to examine cases of a suspicious character which have ocourred in several towns of the province Iran reported to the Spanish Govern- ment that the dieease is. cholera. The Spanish authorities are taking precautionary measures to prevent the spread of the malady. SERIOUS ANTI-JEWISH RIOTS.—FORTY PERSONS

div.p: WOUNDED.

- . VIENNA' Terssnay.--qn the Leopoldstadt, yesterday, serious eats occurred. The partizans of the anti-Semitic candidate, Schneider, attacked some Jews, and afterwards bustled passers-by. Blows were exchanged and blood fiowed. The Carmelite Platz became filled with a howling mob, and free fights commenced, tie roughs generally singling out for their attacks well-dressed persons and women. The police were put tor fight, and the military had to be,calied out. la the meantime the rioters had made raids into a numba of shops kept by .Jews, and the ferocity of their assaults increased. About forty persons were wounded, several seriously, and some arrests were made. DEbTRUCTIVE CYCLONE. . . .
THMESDAY.—A cyclone occurred here yeaterdaV doing damage to the estimited amount of £50,000.

Two lodges were in a Biekly condition, but ,might recover with change of treat- ment The number of members in good standing on the Ist of Febricary last was 3,432 ; initiated between Febtuiry ist eel May, Ist, a. 89 ; admitted by clear- ance card, 53 ; re•instated,..l.2 ; totel 4,016. div.head: ENGLAND IN,ND_ RUSSIA_.
div.p: ENGLAND IN,ND_ RUSSIA_.

THE AFGHAN BOUNDARY SETTLED.. The Daily .21W:s on Saturday stated "on the highest q authority that the reply of the Ruseian Government to theta' counter proposals of her Majesty's Government on the scb- ject of the Afghan frontier was 'received in London on Fri- day, that it involves at acceptance of these proposals, and thus practically settles in a satisfactory manner the whole question of the Afghan boundary. Both Meruchak andTal- fikar remain in the rosse4on e the Ameer. The work to be done by the Frontier-Commission apply only to details. The main features of the delimitation have beeneaually fixed. The negotiations have been canducted on both aides in a most friendly and conciliatory spirit, resulting from a mutual 'desire Wel ct the-cettlement of this at nee time threatening question." On Monday, the seine Ijocreal pub- lished a letter from Lord Granville's secretary saying—" I am desired by Lord Granville to state that the-authority whom you nnete in your issue of this morning has been in- correctly informed as tolhe state of the negotiations with the Russian IC overeat-met in regard to the Afghan frontier. The neeotietions are still going on." Commenting on this, the Daily Pews says:—" The negoticions -with Russia, though not formally' concluded, are approaching comple- tion, and we being condumed on both Melte in the most friendlyucirit. Oa 'Friday M. de Steal bed an interview with Lert: Granville, and on Saturday Lord`kitnberly con- ferred, we believe, with M. Lesser. The letter from Lord Granvitie's privatmoecretary which we putE.sh this morn- ing car The easilyreconciled with the 'statement which we made en Saturday. The English answer to the last com- munication from the Russian Government has not yet been given, bet there is nothing to justify the suspicion that'eny bitch whatever has occurred. lit is of course ob- vious that the settlement of topographichl details involves a very careful examination, and that the controversy be. the two countries cannot be ateolutely closed until there remains no element of doubt inewhat is acceptable to both sides. `But it will be found, when the Government is able to publish an account of recent ,and current transac- tions, that the information we gave en Saturday was sub- stantially correct. We did not say; it will be remembered, 'that 'discussion was at an end, but that Russia had accepted -therauntereproPosals of her MajastY'e Ministers. A representative of the Press Association in an interview with one of the representatives of tbe Powers engaged in I negotiations upon the Russo-Afghan frontier question, was informed that Russia had acceded-to the proposal that the :Zulfikar'Tass and Meruchak shoned be considered Afghan possessions, and Penideh as Russian. Other details were yet to be considered, including the time and place of the meeting of the Demarcation Commissioners, but these would not ii...*ect the settlemeot of the main points already ar- rived at. Sr. 'TEntessIIRO, SUNDAY:a:The last frontier proposals of the-English Government have Ira substance been accepted, and except as to details, some of which, however, are im- portant, while others can only be decided on the spot, the boundary between Russia and Afghanistan may he con- sidered settled. The chief difficulty arose from the Russian claim to Meruchak as part and parcel of the Penjdeh oasis. Another point in dispute was whether the pass of Zulfiaar should be partially or wholly in Afghan hands. English prone-ads maintained the rights of the Ameer in both cases, and the new frontier, therefere, if definitely accepted, will proceed from a point on the Hen i Red, just north of the Pass, to the Murghab north of Meruchak.—Standar d. The accompanying sketch will give our readers an idea of the arrangements come to with regard to the north fron- tier of Afghanistan. The two points between which the joint frontier extended up to November last, and before the 'forward movement of GeneralsKomarofFeegan, were Sarekhs on the Heri Reed and Khoja-Saleb on the river Ones. But these two points were the only absolutely settled points on the frontier. The duty intrusted to the Delimitation Com- mission was to find out how far north, in the direction of a straight line drawn from -Steakles to the Murghab, the Afghan poesessiens extended. The territory farther to the sast—thab le to say between the Murghab and the Oxus— Offered little or no difficulty to the Boundary Commission- ers. It is an almost uninhabited desert of sand. The prac- ticaLquestion turned upon the delimitation of the more fer- tile tract lying between the Hen i Rod on the west and the Murghab on the-east. The whole territory may be roughly de4cribed as,a parallelogram, bounded on the north by the Sarahhs straight line already mentioned ; on Ihessouth by the Paroparnistis Mountains (south of which lies Herat); on the west by the Hen i Rad, or river of Herat and-Sarakhs ; and on the east by the Murghab, or river of Merv. '-From the Sarakhs Ene in the north to the moon' tame in the south the distance is, as the drew flies, about 150 miles. The average breadth of the parallelogram from river to, river is, in a straight line, about 100 miles. Within this area, measuring on a rough calculation, some 15,000 square mile—have taken place the manceuvres and counter- manoeuvres of the Russians and Afghans, which ended in the fight at ,Perajdeb, and which at one time more than seemed to threaten war between the two empires. When Sir Pe,c.q Lninsden started on his mission, the Russians were still outside this area—at any rate, they had not appropria- ted any of it. By the agreementaconcluded on Friday be- tween the two empires, the Russiansare now in possession of nearly two-thirds of it—not, however, tbe richest, en rather the naturally richest portions. The selection of the new boundary has been one of several choices. The fron- tier proposed by M. Lesser started from the Hen i Reid at a epotealled Karez Elias, some twenty miles north of the Herat hills; stretched westwards to Chaman-i-beid on the Knelt river:; and then, turning northwards, it crossed the Murghab at a place a little to the north of Meruchak That is to say, M. Lesear's proposed frontier left Merachuk to the Ameer, but it reserved for Russia the important post of Zulfikar, Ak Robot, and Penjdeb. It will he remembered that Zulfikar and Ak Robat were occupied by the Russians long even before they drove the Afghins out of Penjdeb. After the Penjdelt fight, in short, the Russians were in actual possession of the whole country included within M. Lesser's frontier—the country, the de'imitation of which Russia agreed with England, should be settled ,quietly by a joint commission. The question then came to be, would ltossTa yield any of the positions she had thus eccuPied by force? The reeolt of the negotiations which have been carried on since the battle of Penjdeh is that Russia has yieldst to the English proposal of her withdrawing from the Zulfficar Pass, on the other hand, England—with the Ameer's full eMsent—agrees that Russia shall hold Ponj• deb. Notwithstanding Filday's arrangement, importmt work remains for the Commission of Delimitation. The boundary between the main points will have to be marked •, but this, though perhaps a somewhat laborious process, will be a matter of detail, FURTHER OFFICIAL DESPATCHES. - •

Further correspondence respecting the affairs of Central Asia has beep issued. 'The despatches last published con- cluded just before the 11.2WS of the Russian attack moon the Afghans at Penjdeli had reached this country. The narra- tive is now combined to the cemmenceinett of May, when the two Governments agreed upon a reference to the Sov- ereign of a friendly Power. The delimitation of the fron- tier is scArcely named. The points of importance referred to are the responsibility for the battle of Penideb, the in- terpretation of the Agreement of March 16th, and the ques- tion how the difference of opinion between England and Russia with regard to General Komarofrs proceedings I might hest be decided. The papers present the sight of English statesmen, diplomatists. and generals acting in con• cart to maintain the rights and reputation of Great Britain. The" unhappy incident" of March 30th, when the Afghans were driven over the Kusht, is the point which the arbitra- tor will have to dersrmine. Sir P. Lumsden regards the conduct of General Komaroff as aggressive and unprovoked. &irlo Lumeden 'FM not on the spot, and was not always

correctly informed. But be has been, so far as these de- spatches go, supported by her Majesty's Government, which from the first took a very serious view of the collieion at Penjdeb. Thus, on April Bth, Lord a rativille writes to Sir Edward Thornton 1 "I have to reqcest your Excel- lency to ask the Rassian Government for an explanation of this apparently complete disobAience of the Emperor's orders," while on the same day he informs Sir Pcter Lutneden that " tier Majesy'e Government approve the efforts which he made to prevent the cause of the cellision being due to the Afghans." On April 'l3th Lord Granville informed Sir Edward Thornton of the substance of e con- versation which had passed between himself and T. 21. de Snot This despatch is numbered 1;2. M. de Steal made Certain proposals to Lord Granville, not on the frontier it- self, but on the principle which was to be applied to its settlement. Lord Grancolle remarked on the ambiguity of one of M. de Steal's saggestiens, and wished to know whether it meant that under esecified circumstances the Russian line was to be adopted simptteiter. M. de Staal replied that it did, and Lord Granville at once told 17:9 Excellency that it was imposeitle that we should agree to such a condition." Lord Granville then went ore to urae, on his own account, and cot in defer- ence to Russia, that "it weuld be desirable to reduce as much as possible the limits of 'the inquiry on the spot by a previous understanding between the Governments as to the main points of the frontier line." This was the commence- meut of the negotiations, which have since-teen conducted between Lord Granrille, Lord Kimberley, M. de Steal, and M. Leesar. On April 9th Sir E. Thornton celled upon M. de Were., and spoke in very plain language of the affair at Penjdeh, and the excuses which had been slide for it. Sir' Edward said:—" I alluded,to the cause given in the Gasefle for the attack—namely., 4 the provoking and evidently hos- tile conduct of the Afghans,' and said that it appeared to me insufficient and almost childish (un en/v./if/age), consider- ing the etringent orders which had been issued, that a con- flict was to be avoided by every means." M. de Giers mildly "admitted that as yet the explanation did notxp- pear sufficient." •On April 'loth M. de Glees protested to Sir E. Thornton that the words "unhappy incident" must not be taken to mean that the Emperor or himself admitted the Russian commander to be in the wrong. Sir Edward Thornton answered that the words certainly did not imply it, bat that the fact was se. Sir Edward Thornton' lan- guage is throughout approved by Lord Granville. On April 17th M. de Giers, rather late in the day, referred to the military appearance of the English Commission, against which he had no docbt previously protested, as one of "tire facts leading to the incident At -A,k Tepe " or Penjdeh. Lord Graoyille had little difficulty in disposing of this plea. "We should have regarded." he wrote to Sir Edward Thorn- ton on April 19th," a Russian escort of sufficient strength in compeny with a Commissioner as a guarantee for order, and we hoped that Use Russian Governmeet would have re- garded a !doltish escort-in the-same way." When the ques- tion of arbitration came to be discussed, the Russian Government was-dead against it. As soon as M. de Steal could be broughtio contemplate it at all, he suagested the German Emperor. ;Lord Granville!s reply is: "I said that the choice of tire Emperor of tGermany was a very natural one for his Excellency to think of, both on account of his Majesty's relationship to the Emperor of Russia and because of the intimate-relations hetween the two countries. After this Lord Granville went -on-to-say that he had no objec- tion. These despatches close with the agreement for a reference of the covenant and its &Bend breach to arbitra- tion, and for the temporary neutralisation of Penjdeh. Since that time the bases of reference have been fix,d, and the King of Denmark has been appointed arbitrator. The correspondence shows that Lord Granville his scored a con- siderable diplomatic victory, and reflects the very highest credit upon Sir Edward Thorzton, who has taken a tone equally courteous and -firm. CONSTANTINOZLE, TIIESDLY.—Sir Peter Lumsden, who left to-day for London, via Varniehas had no political inter- view during his stay in the Turkish capital. The Press Association understands that the final settle- moot of the negotiations between M. tie Steal and M. Lesser and Errl Granville and the Reel of Kimberley far the de- limitation of the Afghan frontier is now in view. The Le- gotiations were advanced a stage on Tuesday, when Lord Kimberley came to town specially to confer upon the details still requiring to be settled. It is ex- pected in official circles that by Monday next Ministers will be enabled to state in Parliament that the basis of an agreemeet has been arrived at as to the instructions to be given to the officers detailed to mark out the boundary in Afghanistan. AFGHAN FRONTIER NEGOTIATIONS.

ST. PETERSBURG. THIIESDAY.—The negotiations between England and Russia are being carried on in the most friendly manner, and net, as has been stated by some for- eign papers, with a certain decree of acerbity. They will, however, still occupy a considerable time, as no definite arrangement has yet been arrived at. Russia puts forward no demands; but makes certain proposals which it is believed here will be met by England in a conciliatory spirit.

Dishes, Saucepans, Guns, Urge. Hones, Ac. Packets Olik/ FENNY and U, wards.—Adet On Tuesday morning, during a fire in Fitzroy-square, London, a lodger in that house was burned to death. ADAMS V. COLERIDGE.—In the Court of Appeal, on Thursday, Mr. Adams, the plaintiff in the libel case of Adonis v. Coleridge, appealed against the decision of Mr. Justice Manisty in giving judgment for the defendant after the jars, had returned a verdict for the plaintiff. The argu- ments were not concluded. ATTEMPTED Otrrnans.—Early on Thursday morning a tin canister containing a quantity of gunpowder was placed upon a window-sill at Leesfield Viceroy, near Oldhem, the residence of the Rev. Canon Whittaker. The explosive material was fired in some way which is not yet clear, but no great damage resulted. The cause of this abominable outrage is not known, and there is no trace of the culprits. THE FATAL KICKING AT OLDHAM.—At Oldham, on Thursday morning, Patrick Graham Was charged with the wilful murder of his wife, Mary Graham. 'the prisoner, it is alleged, kicked the deceased in his house at Cireenacres Hill last Fridry, and she died from the eff.,cts of his violence on Tuesday. The chief constable asked for a remand uotil the inquest was held, and the prisoner was remanded until Monday. FATAL FIRE REAR BOLTON.—A WOMAN RoASTED.—A sad domestic c rtestrophe occurred early on Thursday morn- ing, at Chew Moor, near Balton. A cottage occupied by a family named Hibbert, and an old woman of seventy, the mother of the wife, seven persons in all, was discovered to be on lire about two o'clock. Hibbert, who is a collier, at great risk, rescued the whole of the inmates, with the ex- ception of the old woman. The cottage was burnt to the ground, the roof and floors falling in before the Balton Fire Brigade arrived. The brigade prevented the destruction of adjoining property already alight. When it was possible to enter the cottage, the charred remains of the unfortunate women were discovered by the firemen's dog. She was completely roasted, having probably been suffocated when attempting to escape. The whole of the furniture was destroyed. MRS. S. A.
