WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. ' The ordinary monthly meeting of this body was held On Tuesday evening in the Council Chamber at the Town flail, the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presiding, and there being also present Aldermen Burgess, Holmes, Kean, Davies, and Wet ster, Councillors Broadbent, Bolton, Burgess, Roberts, W. Pierpoint, Dixon, Hutchinson, Fleming, Green- ing, Platt, Sutton, Taylor, Marsh, Francomb, Jolley, Mackie, and J. E. Wright ; Messrs. W. H. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), Chorley (borough treasurer), Longdin (boreugh surveyor), and Paterson (gas manager.) THE FAWCETT MEMORIAL. The MAYOR reported the receipt of a communication from a committee in London, inviting the Council to sub- scribe to the Notional Fawcett Memorial, one which, he said, would enlist the sympathies of all of them. If any gentleman would like to give a contribution he should be glad to receive it, or if it was wished that a sum of money should be voted—if they bad the power to do so—he for ene should be happy to do it. Councillor BROADBENT : Is there any precedent for

that? The MAYOR It would appear to me that if we can vote money towards the ship can.ll, that we might with great propriety contribute towards this. Councillor BROADBENT: Greater propriety. I think so

too. The"Matzm : The Town Clerk advises us that we can- not do it, but if any gentleman should like to contribute I should betappy to receive his name. THE TRAFFIC IN SANKEY. STREET. On the consideration of the minutes of the Watch Com- mittee, which were proposed for adoption on the motion of the Miertort, seconded by COIMICiIIOr BROADBENT, CUM- cillor Dexoer again referred to the traffic in Sankey-street on Sunday evenings. He thought that the obstructions in the traffic he had to complain of would be done away with if people in that street would keep on the move. A-Merman BURGESS suggested that it would be an im- provement to have notices asking people" to keep to the right." It was indiscriminate walking, right and left, that ver7 wenerally caused obstrueions. The MAYOR: It would in a great measure help to miti- gate the evil. The matter haa been brought before Mr. Ent, and he said he woull not relax his endeavours to keep the street as orderly as possible. STREET IMPROVEMENT END LIGHTING COMMITTEE. Councillor BROADEENT proposed, and Councillor PLATT -ceconded, the adoption of the report of this committee.. Councillor W. PrEcaeoeterr said that a number of plans were recommended for approval. A fire had occurred at the premises of Mr. Lamb, in Wash-lane, a great portion of the ' building being destroered, and he noticed that the premises were being relmilt in their ancient form, which was very unsanitary. He wiehed to ask had any action been taken to see that the buildiog that would be re-erected would con- form to the rules of the Sanitary Authority. Councillor BROtLDBENT, in reply, said that the building was not being rebuilt—the new roof was being placed on the old walls, and he thooght that they had no power to in- sist upon those conditions that they should do if it was en- tirely a new building. The sanitary arrangements of the property were defective, and the surveyor would keep his eye on the arrangements, but he was sure the Rector of Grappenhall, who represented the property, would be willing and anxious to adopt such suggestions as the Borough Sur- veyor thought •neeessary. The minutes were then adopted. _
THE dEELLTH OF THE Boaorae.

The Sanitary Committee reco nmended that a report o the Medical Officermf Health (Dr. Gornall) for 1884 be ap- proved. The report stated that during the year 1884 the number of births 'registered in the borough amounted to 1,909, of which 995 were males and 914 females. This was an increase of 39 upon the births recotded in the previous year, and 110 more than the average of the previous five years (1879 to 1883). Of the 1,909 births 1,728 were reg- istered in the Warrington Registration District, and 181 in that of Latchford. The birth-rate was 42.9 per 1.000 of the populatien, against 43, the average of the previous five years. The total number of deaths recorded in the borough during the year 1884 amounted to 953, 868 being regis- tered in the Warringtcm and 85 in the Latchford Registration District. This number included 8 that took place in the Fever Hospital, 9 in the Infirmary, and 82 in the Work- house Hospital. From the total of 953 deaths must be de- ducted 8 which occurred in the Workhouse of persons admitted from parts of the Warrington Uoion outside the municipal boundary, and 2of strangers who died in the berough. The remaining 943 represents the actual number of deaths to be debited te the bormigh. The rate of mor- tality for the year was equivalent to 21.19 per 1,900 persons living, on an estimated population of 44.482 to the middle of the year, being .42 per 1,000 lower than 1883. Com- pared with the mean mortality of the preceding ten years, the death-rate shows a reduc'ion of 2.3 per 1,000, and a saving of 102 human livesdaring the year 1884. No deaths were due to small-pox, and scarlet fever continued steadily to decline. During the year only four deaths were regis- tered in the borough from this disease. The number of patients admitted to the Infectious Diseases Hospital dui, leg the year was 56, the number admitted since the Im- provement Act received the Royal assent being 821, and the total number admitted since the hospital was opened in May, 1877, being 898. Daring the year 1,753 articles had been disinfec'ed. The cost of maintenance dur:ng the year was £1,141 4s. Alderman BURGESS moved the confirmation of the min- utes, commending the Medical Officer's report to the care- ful attention of the Council, and Councillor SUTTON secon- ded the motion. Councillor MAMIE congratulated the committee on the result of the year's labours. When they read that no less than 100 precious lives had been preserved as against an average of ten years, or 1,000 lives in that ten years, they could not but express the warmest thanks- to all who had had to do with preserving the health and sanitation of the borough.. At the same time there existed a great amount of infant mortality. In round numbers one-half of the deaths were of children under five years of age, and one-fourth under one year old. No less than 13 sewer cases had turned up again this year. He thought it was also well to call attention to the fact that out of the £1,141 expended at the hospital £llO was for coals and £B5 for gas. He thought it just possible that the consumption of those pro- ducts had been out of all keeping with what we should have in our own homes, and more certainly when it was con- sidered that there had only been 56 patients. It might be, however, that there was some system of keeping the rooms continually heated and lighted. Councillor Dixon asked if the committee had received a communication from a solicitor with regard to the pro- posed depot in the North-East Ward ? Alderman BURGESS, replying, said that emanations of sewer gas should be suppressed as much as possible, but all sufficiently educated in sanitary matters would have come to the conclusion that it was better that gas should be liberated at distances such as was the case in Warriagton, than that it should be kept confined in sewers and eventually driven into some or other of the houses in the town. There were times when the sewers were made foul, and the emana- tions were bad, not through the sewage of the town, but by some of the manufacturers at given periods turning into the sewers that which never ought to go there. He w,s glad attention had boon called to the coals and gas at the hos- pital, and was free to confess that it seemed to him that so far as the gas was concerned the amount was large, consider- ing that there was so little doing at the hospital. That question would have to be gone into, and also the question of the coals, although the medical superintendent might rrquire a certain degree of heat to be maintained. He WAS reminded that the disinfecting stove consumed a large amount of gas, and that was no doubt an explanation of the large amount consumed. The committee had bad one or two letters of rather a threatening character with reference to the depot in the North Ward, but they had the instruc- tion of the Council to proceed with the work, and dld not know that it was within their province to take notice of any threats while following out those instructions. The minutes were passed without further discussion. THE PAVING OF STREETS. A recommendation of the Paving and Sawerage Commit- tee that the plan for the paving of Thynne-street be ap- proved, and that the Town Clerk be instructel to serve the necessary notices for the completion of the street, provoked considerable discussion, and Alderman KFAN, in proposing the adoption of the committee's report, anticipated objec- tions that would be taken to it. He was sure, he satd, that any person objec ing to the paving of that street would be sorry if in a few months afterwards some of the families in that neighbourhood were stricken down with fever. He be- lieved that the Weject of the opposition was the expenses and hardship that would be incurred by the owners. Dr.

Gornall, in 1882, pointed out that several streets in that neighbourhood were detritnental to health, Ti.ynne-street being included, and in 1883 the foundations and for tpath were put down. The cost now would only be £5 153 per house.
Councillor TbYLOR seconded the prposition. Councillor PixoN moved as an amendment that the minutes be confirmed with the exception of the one refer- .
ring to Tilynne-streA: He urged that traffic in ,that street

was not heavy, and that it was in a better conditkm than eiiher Bridge-street, or Sankey-street. Parker-street and Arnley-street were anything but satisfactory, and he failed to see why Thynne-street should be singled out. By in- sisting on certain streets being paved, the committee had inflicted serious injury on several persons, who yet suffered painfully through it. The MAYOR read a memorial from owners of property in the street asking that the paving should le left over for the present. The street, he said, was better than many in the town having ten times the traffic Aroley-s.reet its,lf being little better than a common ditch, and it was hoped that as a matter of justice the Council would give attention to those streets which were in worse condition than Thynne• . .

aireei, and were more necessary for general traffic. Councillor JOLLEY seconded the amendment, and, in answer to the IN.Layor, said that the Loan Company had no interest in the matter, lie asked the Council to let Thynne•

street alone unt.l. Arpley-street, the main street, on Which the other abuts, was done. He thought they were working on wrong lines. They took ten years to make Bath•street. with ten times the traffic, and in two years asked to have a . . . . .
street that could not be Used because' the main ktreet it
abutted upon was so bad. Councillor BURGBSS thought some system should be adop-
ted for making the paving a private ;trees more easy thin was at present the ease, and that the expense should be ex- tended over some time. Unless some reason was given for
not paving Arpley-street, ha should not favour the pro- position, as he thou6lat both streets should be taken at

ORM Councillor WRIGHT, in supporting the amendment, con- sidered it inconsistent to force the paying of Tiiy nne-stNet on the owners of property in the present state of aff Airs. It was as good as Sankey-street, and he thought it a hardship to unduly press. a working-man who was trying to gain a

house to himself. Councillor ROBERTS also supported the amendment. He could testify to what had been said in reference to the con- dition of Arolev-street. It was a disgrace to any civilised community. The sanitary arrangements were utterly out of order, and the street itself was a perfect nuisance at all times when the weather was not fine. He could not under- stand on what principle they worked with regard to the allotment of the time at which certain streets shauld be made. Here was one only still partially Luilt upon orthred immediately to be paved, whereas streets that bad been used for years bad been left untouched. He thought that some definite course of action should be laid down, so that pro- perty owners could have some idea when they commenced building, when they would be likely to be called upon to make the streets. At some other time he should move that the terms of payment be amended, so as to make them easier, as he thought that the titne should be extended and the payments made in instalments.

Councitlor ltlensa conbidered that if property owners were going to be let off in the manner suggested in the case of Thynne-street, they should have many similar ap- plications. Councillor BROADBENT thought the opponents of the minute had made out a good case, but was of opinion, not- withstanding, the sooner a street was paved the better. But the circumstances of this case were rather peculiar. It was admitted that Arplev-street was more in need of paving, and therefore he thought the committee might do well to wait a little and get Arpley.street paved first. Alderman BmiOnss supported the minutes. He had seen that committee thwarted on a recent occasion, and very im- properly towarted. He referred to the matter of Bridge. street, which was caused by the instrumentality of a memo- rial. They were evidently getting to legislate by memorial. If the committee had not been actuated by the fear of press- ing too hardly upon people, it would not be only the public streets, such as Thynne-street and Arpley-street, that they would desire to pave, but the Council would be urged to pave the back passlges to premiere, and not leave them as they were now, in a condition prejudicial to health. Who that had been five years in that Council did not know that there was an insuperable difficulty with reference to Arpley- street ? Was it not at least an open secret that there 'WAS an understood arrangement with Lord Winmarleigh with refer- ence to the paving of the street? Had the committee undertaken it at their charge, it would have been squander- ing the public money. If the committee thought no more could be done with respect to the agreement, and accepted the responsibility of making the street, he was sure that the Council would support them in their work. The work of paving was dragging behind, and that state of affairs must come lo an end. He thought the Council should have con- fidence in the committee they appointed. Councillor Pwarr said that he should be glad if 913 chairman of the committee could see his way Vç withdraw the recommendation for a time. The question had been , asked as to whether the people in this street were connected with any building society. He considered that than build- ing societies there were no more useful institutions in this country, and there were no class of people more deserving consideration at the hands of the Council than the people who were striving to get a house of their own. From the number of names appended to the memorial he should think that in this Case nearly alt the inhabitants of the etreet were their own landlords, or were striving to become

- _ so. That was a great argument why they should be allowed more latitude than a large property owner, who was required to pave the streets in the interests of his tenants. Alderman DAVIES suggested that a unanimous vote might be obtained if the chairman of the committee would give an undertaking that, notwithetandmg the passing of the resolution, nothing should be done with regard to Thynne- i street until it was executed as a whole in conjunction with Arploy-stret t. Alderman Hotaras supported the minutes. When a man, he said, purchased land for building he knew that he would have to make toe street, and after a street was paved no one would ,be called upon for payment for something like 12 months, so that they bad time for preparation. Councillor GREENING supported the minutes, thinking that if the street had been left for another year or two the same objection would have been raised. No one would pay for street making if they could help it, and he had no doubt that the committee had good reasons for taking the course that they did in the present case. If they paved Thynne- street it would be an inducement to the owner of the other street to carry out his agreement with the Corporation made some years ago, The MAYOR expressed sympathy with the suggestion thrown out by Councillor Roberts, that the Council should authorise payment for paving by instalments, instead of in a lump sum. Alderman KEAN having replied to the remarks made by other speakers, the report was adopted in its entirety.

The minutes of the Museum,Library, and Arts Committee, contaiaed an offer tram Mr. William Eeamont, of Orford Hall, to present to the Art Gallery, where he thought it would have a fitting abode, the large picture of the Royal Psalmist, singing the 147th Psalm to his harp, of which he was uovr become for,the second time,the owner. The Ceuncil decided to accept the offer, with cordial thanks to Mr. Boa- moot, to whose generosity fitting tributes were paid by Alderman Webster, Councillors Sutton and Jolley, and the IMayor, the latter of whom rernatked that it was a singular Icircumstance that Mr. Beamont first purchased the picture and presented it to St. Paul's Church, and then when it was not of use for the church, most generously re-purchased it and now made a present of it to the Art Uallery. 015 COMMITTEE.

This committee recommended, amongst other things, that in order to meet the riquiremects of the Paving and Sewer- age and Sanitary Committees hi working the ejectors for the Latchford Sewerage Scheme, and the Intercepting Depots, two new boilers be purchased and erected at the works, and that such committee be charged a fair proportion of the cost of working and use of the boilers, to be ascer- tained after three months' operation. Alderman HOLMES proposed, and Councillor Wuroirr seconded the adoption of the minutes. Councillor W. PiEueorerr said that he was confirmed in the opinion he had formed that the boilers were necessary for the collection and removal scheme. He believed that it I was a feasible scheme, bat the reason he had for opposing it was simply the fact that he wanted the Sanitary Com- mittee to show that they were able to deal with the material properly when they got it to Longford, bofore going to that expense. He moved as an amendment that the minutes be passed with the exception of the recommendation re- ferred to. Councillor BOLTON seconded the proposition. Remarks were made on the subject by Councillor Fran- comb, Alderman Burgess, Councillor Platt, Councillor Sutton, Alderman Davies, Councillor Greening, and Alder- man Holmes. On a vote being taken, the original motion was carried, there only voting for the amendment Councillors Platt, W. Pierpoint, and Bolton. Councillor Dexote was so' mating a motion that the pub- lic analyst be directed to analyse the gas once every month, and report the result thereof to the General Purpose 3 TE - inittee, and that the necessary appatatus be purchased for that purpose, when it was discovered that there was no quorum, and the meeting broke up.

GENERAL GORDON.-Tht suzgeetion that a largo hospital ehould be erected at Port Said as a memorial to the late General Gordon has been ab mdoned, but it is recommended that some hut or other slight form ef hospital should be en. couraged at Port Said, though not by way of memorial to the General. A IsIEW DEFENSIVE AGENT.—The admiralty have accep- ted the invention et a petty r flicer on bard the Vernon, by means of which a steam pinnace containing a heavy charge of gun-cotton cin be launched without a crew and submerged for an indefinite p.rioci, the charge being camo. ded when desired, before an enemy becomes aware of the presence of the craft. A MAD CAPIA,IN.—A boy beloneiug to a barque lying off Whitstable rowed ashore to tne Coastenard Station, on Saturday, and reported that the captain, William Usher, had attempted to throw him oveiboard, and, failing in this, jumped overboard himself, but got back again. An officer of the coastguard boarded the barge and found the captain pacing the deck as thouo raving mad. He was secured and brought ashore, and has since been removed to an asylum._ . .

CHURCH DEFENCE IN SCOTLAND.—An organisation, irides pendent of the Established Church Committee, was formed in Edinburgh on Saturday. Seine difference arose, and a Number of gentlemen left before the resoletions were sub- mitted. It was agreed to form a National Committee of De- fence, being an organisation of the people of Scotland in de- fence of the principle of the national recognition of religion, and of the essential and fundemental conditions of the union of Scotland and England, A LADY P ninsentererte CANDIDLTE.—A deputation A from the committee of the Cumber, ell Radical Club have waited upon their hon. president, Miss Helen Taylor, asking her to become a Parliamentary candidete in the Radical in- terest for North Camberwell at the general election. Itt reply, Miss Helen Taylor said it was true that there was no law to prevent a woman sitting in Parliament—in fact, one had taken her seat in the femme beam. now. Eventually Miss Taylor consented to accept the inviratioe, and to go to - the poll. REDUCTION OF RE/s'T AND IMPROVEMENT OF LAND.—The Duke of Devonshire has intiamtel his interition of allowing to all his farm tenants in the disti ict of Buxton, with the exceptien of those holding 0 acceommdarion land," and those who were not affected by the revaluation in 1870, the whole of one year's rent on comlition that the amount IS expended in lime and applied to the land. Tenants who have only entered upon their holdings since Lady Day, lan, will be allowed six months' rent. ATTEMPTED DOUBLE MITRDER.—At Kent Police Court OR Saturday, William 1). English, aged 30, was charged with attempting to murder Cornelia Oosr, aged ten, by beating her about the head with a lath hammer, and also with attempting to murder Fred Edward Ricearda, aged two, in a similar manner, on the 14th hottest% It was stated that the prisoner was somewhat the worse for drink when he attacked the children, and that he had always appeared to be very fond of the little girl. The prisoner was committed for trial. ATTEMPT TO BRIBE a MAGIS MATE. The Mayor of Stratford-on-Avon' at the Police Court there on Monday, said an attempt had been made to bribe him by a defendant who was then before the court. The defendant had writ- ten offering to present him with a valuable oil painting in his possession, if he would lock over a promcntion for eel- ling drink without a license. The defendeet having been convicted, the Bench said they would consiller whether he had not forfeited the license by attempting to bribe a magistrate. STATUE OF THE LATE LORD FREDERICK CATENDISH.--. The Lord-Lieutenant of Ireland Las bent a letter to the Mayor of Barrow, intimating that if the necessary arrange- ments can be made he will he prepared to unveil the statue of the late Lord Frederick Cevendish, to be erected in the I Town Hall Square at Barrow, during tee present mouth. A special committee of the sewn Council has been an- pointed to make these-arrangements at au early date. The. statue, which is the work of Mr. B. uce Joy, is in Farrow waiting to be raised on its pedestal, which is already erec- ted. A STREET FLOODED WITH BEFTL—A. despatch from. Pittsburg U.S. dated the 3rd ult., says :—Eerly yesterday morning Wainwrieht's Brewery, at ths corner of Thirty- sixth and Charlottemtreets, caved in, and the streets in the neighboterbood te-day were filled with flowing beer. There were over 10,500 barrels of the her stored on the upper floors, and the extra heavy pressure caueed the beams to give way. The rafters forced the walls, and in a few minutes almost the entire buildiug was in the cellar. All the machinery is wrecked. 'The loss is over 100,000 dol- lars. Tke air in the neighbourhood of the brewery was filled with the smell of beer. In some places the beer gathered in pools, and the people dipped them dry with, !cans. Thousands vierted the SUES of fits wreck, and many who came sober went away drnok. Toe police were kept busy in dispersing the crowds, which seemed to delight in. this novel method of beer•driing. THE ALLEGED TRIPLE MURDER IN COUNTY CORK —At Castletown, Roche, County Cork, on Monday. Wm. Sheehan and David Browne were charged with the wilful murder of Hannah, Catherine, and Thee. Sheehan, whose bodies were found in a well at Cestletovsn, Roche.—Dr. Quinlan de- posed to the examination of the remains. He believed them to be those of three adults—two females and one male.— Eliza Maynes, sister of Catherine Seeehan, sail she did not I know what became of her sister, and did net believe she would have gone away without acquainting her.—Mary Healy deposed that since the disappearance of the deceased she had spoken to the prisoner Sheehan about his mother,. and he always said she was all right.—E.videace was afters, wards given as to the finding of the bodies, and John Shea-- ban, brother of the prisoner William, was then examined. He stated that on the day prier to the disappearance of the membere of his family, he attended a religious service at his mother's house. No mention was then made of any intention on their part to leave the place. He never saw them after- wards. On the evening of the following day he again called to see his mother, and was informed by his brother that she and the others had gone away on a hired cm. The prisoner. was engaged to be married to a young woman of whom hiss mother climapproved, but be married her. Witness was present at the wedding, and received from his brother £lOO out of the wedding portion of the bride. The btide's father, the prisoner Browne, told him that £I.FO, forming the tee minder of the wedding portion, Lad boon paid to bie (Shoe- hen's) mother.—The inquiry was adjoureed. FARMERS AND POLITICS. A meeting of the Stefferd- shire Chamber of Agriculture was held on naturdey at Stafford, for the consideration eneinly of the question "whether and what action should be taken by chambers of agriculture at the approaching eeneral election to ascertain the views of candidates on agricultural questions." The President (Mr. T. Carrington Smith), mid he had long been of opinion that farmers as a class had been afraid of taking their proper share in political elf ors by the cry of no politic." It was right enough to exclude party politics from agricultural societies and from the dinners which ac- company agricultural ehows, but chambers of agriculture stood on quite a different footine. If there was any reason for their existence it was that they should lead their mem- bers to take an interest in general pcntical questions. Such had been the case in the past. When qeestions affectine agri- culture had Men the subject ef leaislation chambers of agri- culture had discussed those quesiene and they had on several occas:ons influenced the /tenon of Pasliarneet. Un- less they took their proper piece in political affeirs and wielded their rightful influence farmers would be pushed aside by the new electorate, and they would whnn it was too late eeplore their indifference. A resolution, moved by the president and seconded by Mr. W. Sampson, was carried de- claring it to be the opinion of the cha.mber that it is desir- able to take action at the approaching election in order to aecertain the views of candidatee on agricultural questions. The preparation of the queslions to be submitted to cireli- dates was left in the hands of the council. The President disclaimed any desire to make the chamber an instrument for the promotion of party pinnies. The Worcestershire Chamber of Agriculture adopted on Saturday by eight votes to three (several members remaining neutral) a de- claration in favour of the imposition of protective duties on all importa from abroad. I goes to Russia, and that is---not to put too ' fine a point upon it---because the AMEER cares nothing about its retention. It is well known that the inhabitants of the Penjdeh district are of a mixed race, and there is so much turbulent Turkoman blood amongst them that ADDUR RAHMAN may be excused if he is not anxious to take upon himself the trouble of keeping them in order. The place is of no great value either from a strate- gical point of view. But it is otherwise with Zulficar ; the possession ot that pass is of great importance to the Ruler of Afghanistan. Meruchak is valuable on account of its fertility, and it lies so well on the way to Herat from the north that it was a good stroke of diplomacy to arrange that it, too, shall be Afghan rather than Russian territory. These major points hav- ing been settled, it is not likely that any serious difficulty will arise as to minor details. The KING of DENmARE has accepted the high office of arbitrator as to the Penjdeli incident; but the issue has been so narrowed that it should not be difficult for him to give a decision which both parties may accept without either being dishonoured. There are some bellicose politicians who afect to be ashamed of the Government for suggesting arbitration; they would rather, if there was any dispute, that we should "fight it out." They do not see that, as a nation is but an aggregation of individuals, if it is wise in in- dividuals who have disputes to refer the issue 1, to a third party, there is the same room for ,the exercise of wisdom in international quar- rels. To be consistent, these sanguinary citi- zens should "fight it out" in civil life. When they have a dispute, for instance, as to a commercial transaction, instead of agreeing to abide by the decision of BROWN or JONES, or a County Court Judge, they ought rather to "set to" in the street, and account him right who first breaks the other's head The absurdity of such a mode of reference is ob- vious now-a-days to most men ; and when the thirty-five millions in Great Britain who, as CARLYLE has it, are "mostly fools," get rid of some of their folly they will begin to perceive that it is as absurd for nations to fight as it is for individuals. Mean- time we must not neglect to encourage such statesmen as Mr. GLADsTONE and Lord GRANVILLE by saying a word in due season when they have done something to show that they are good as well as great men. We are a long way yet off the Mil- lennium, but we may at least cherish a hope for the time— When the vrar•drum throbs no longer, and the battle 18. g is furled In the Parliament of man—the federation of the world.

aETON-KARR, the Conservative candi- date for St. Helens, seems to feel that he was hard hit when the barrenness of his politica I programme, as revealed in his first speech. was exposed by the press. He has hastened to cover up his defects, having addressed two meetings during the past week, but, although he has in some degree hidden them, they are there ; his " winnowed raggedness" is still apparent to those who have eyes to see. His views on Sunday Ciosing are of the hviest kind. He is "in favour of any measure cal- culated to promote morality and temperance, providing it does not interfere with the liberty of the subject." What does this mean---anything, or nothing? Is Mr. SETON.I KARR so utterly raw as a politician that he has not made up his mind on such a promin- ent question as Sanday Closing ? If so, , he had better make way for someone else, and come again when he has cut his wisdom tooth. Or is he dodging the issue? In , either case he is unworthy of the confidence of the electors of St. Helens. He is willing, if elected, to "consult the views and wishes of his constituents." Wonderful I Mr. KARR has---to use the Tory style of speech---pros- trated himself before the Caucus, and now he does not object to become "a mere dele- gate," if they will. only elect him. But why not consult the views of the electors before he is elected? Is he afraid of having to give a definite answer on such questions as that of gunday Closing ? With regard to the foreign policy of the Government, all he can do is to denounce it in "vague generalities." "Peace at any price "is not, he says, a policy that the Conservatives could approve. Just so; but this is what the Americans would call "fooling around " the subject. If he believ-s that the Government have made badly out, diplomatically, in pre- serving the peace with Russia, let him say so, and adduce, if he can, something like argu- ment in support of his contention. We challenge him to take this course, but we fear argument is not, as the hangman would say, in his line. Referring, at the meeting on Tuesday night, to the agitation for the aboli- tion of the Game Laws, Mr. KARR said a reform of this kind would throw gamekeepers and watchers out of employment, and many of them would be thrust to the Verge of starvation. Really, such reasoning as this is childish. We shall next be asked to resist the temperance movement, because if suc- cessful, publicans and barmen will be " thrust to the verge of starvation" to say nothing of policemen and judges and jailors being "thrown out of employment." The Conser- vatives of St. Helens must have great faith in the gullibility of the new electors if they think they will be content to gulp down such sophistry. Mr. SEION-KARR is either in his "salad days" himself, or takes the newly- enfranchised to be the greenest of green things. They must teach him a lesson, and let it be seen that they are wider awake than I he takes them to be.

THERE has been a good deal of discussion, which has engendered not a little heat, on the increase of the duty on spirits, wine, and beer, as part of the Budget proposals of, the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER. The payer of income -tax seems to have taken meekly to his burden; if he has grumbled, it has been in such a low tone that he has not been heard. But the drinkers of whisky have been spirited, not to say noisy, in their style of complaint, and they have been listened to. Mr. CHILDERS announced in the House of Commons last night that, las he would not be called upon to spend 1 the whole of the Vote of Credit for eleven millions, he proposed that the duty on British and foreign spirits should be one shilling, instead of two shillings per gallon, as at first resolved upon. There would be no change in the resolution as' to the wine duty or the duty on beer, though as to the latter, it was stated that the increase would expire on the 31st of May next. Scotland and Ireland as whis- ky drinkers have been humoured : they have won this round, while as to the wine drinkers --- well, they can afford to pay for whetting their whistle with this particular tipple. The increase in the duty on beer is so small that it will not affect the consumer; and we venture to say there is still such a mar-

LUNACY AT WIDNRS.—By on order ef the Widnes magis- trates Mr. Scannell, relieving officer, has con .reyed to Rain- hill Asylum Mary Ann Fox, 36 years of age, who lived at 95, Midwood-street, Widnes. The woman has been known to the police for years as an incurable drunkii,d,-and dur- ing the Wnitsunticle holidays she drunk to such an excess that she became a raving lunatic. In her frenzy She smashed pearly all the goods in the house, and frequently threatened to take her own life.

DIEGLECt OF FAMILY AT RUNCORN.—Joseph Lowe was I brought before the Runcorn magistrates, oa Thursday, charged with deserting his wife arid children. From the Wridence of Thomas Houghton, collector, it appeared that the prisoner's wiro and children had been inmates of the Workhouse since 220 d January, 1881, and during that time no trace of his whereabouts could be discovered, and he had not contributed anything to their maintenance. On Wed- nesday night he arrived in Runcorn and was immediately anprehemled by P.S. Walls,. He was sentenced to 21 days' hard labour.

THE VICAR OF WIDNES ON THE BIBLE.—The annual meeting of the Widnes Auxiliere of the British and Foreign !Bible Seciety was held in the National Schools, Waterloo- ! road, on Tuesday evening. There was only a poor attend- ance. The Rev. J. Wright Williams, vicar, presided, and he was slum nted by the Revs. J. Symons (deputation) and C. Reeifii r. The Chairman, in a brief address, observed upon the fact that the more strongly the foundation of Bible truths was assailed by the sceptical and the sneering , tee more firmly rooted did they become. The Rev. J. Symons spoke upon the extent of the work of the society in the various ceuntries of the world, describing the society as the granary of mi,.sionary enterprise. The Rev. R. Harper read the report. He stated that 'the receipts amounted to £l5 lde 111, includiog a balance in hand of 10e 3d at tbe commencement of the year. Subscriptions and donatione amounted to a 10a 6d, Mrs. Itebieeon haying collected .£2 Is and Wee R. Hudson £4 9s 6d. The expenses amounted to £4 Bs, the donation to the parent society was £lO. The vote of thanks was seconded by the Rev. C. Rumfitt, and carried. F.IIICIDE AT FRODSHAM BRIDGE.—AR inquest was held by Mr. Churton, the county coroner, at the Ridge Inn, Frod- sham Bridge, on Mender, on the bode- of Thomas Made, who committed suicide by banging himself on Saturday.— Sareh Dean said deceased lived next door to her on the quay. He hid suffered from rheumatism, and had not done any work for three years, and was physically unfit for work. She last saw deceased at nine o'clock on Fri- day night. She had noticed a change in his manner during the past three weeks, and on Friday evening when she took him something to eat, he told her.to put it away, as he did not know what he should do The de- ceavd lived with Thomas Ashbrook,and two children of the witness also slept in the same hose. On Saturday morn. ing the children were liter than usual, and she went at eight o'clock to see where they were, and then saw the de- ceased suspended be a rope from a beam in the back kitchen. She at once obtained assistance, and the body was out down by Richard Horton. The deceased appeared to have been dead for some time evtien cut down.—The jury returned a verdict of " Committed suicide while in a state of tempor- ary insanity." _ _

SECOND STARR BOWEETT BUILDING SOCIETY FOR WIDNES —A second Starr Bowkett Building Society was inaugurated in Widnes on Monday evening, when a public meeting was held in the National Schools, Waterloo-road. Captain Btunner presided, and he was sepported on the platform by Mr. John Ba-croft, of It atnsbottom (agent to Mr. Starr), Mr. S Owens. and Mr. T. J. Peters. Thera was a fair attendance. The chairman observed that the first society during the four years of its existence hal been very successful, and was now in a prosperous and sound condition.—Mr. Barcroft then delivered an address in which he incidentally referred to the advantages of the practice of thrift and the means adopted by the Government to foster these habits in the people. He argued that the Starr Bow- kett societies offered a better, a safer, and a readier means of saving than any other society, and gave to their m3mbers a larger return than could be obtained elsewhere upon the same sum. In explaining the rules and regulations of the society he stated that the entrance fee was is. and the pay- ment per share of £lOO, sixpence per week. When £27 81 had been paid too the member was entitled to a loan of £lOO for 12/ years free of interest, but he might obtain an ap- priation by ballot years before he paid that sum. Only four shares could b 3 taken in a group, but any number of shares could be taken. A member wishing to withdraw his sub- scriptians could not do so until t° society had been in ex- istence rive years. Mr. Barcroft also explained that if a member could not pay his weekly subscriptioas regularly either through sickness or loss of employment, the rules provided that he should not be fined. Other advantages having been pointed out, the usual votes of thanks were ac- corded the Chairman and Mr. Barcroft. A WIDNES HUSE 4,ND'S WORS.—TIDI SALVATION ARIVY AND BOISE Hosker, a well-dressed working- man, appeared before Mr. W. L. Evans, at Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, to answer a charge of threatening to beat and ill-treat his wife Sarah.—The complainant, a young woman, commenced to weep on entering the witnese- , box and said she was willing to withdraw the case if her husband would make it up with her and promise not to assault her again—The husband did net manifest any dis- position to agree to this proposition, and the case proceeded. —The complainant said on Sunday, the 24th, a man en- tered the kitchen of the house and asked her husband for some tobacco. She shouted from upstairs "Don't take it off him, as he will talk about it after he has given it to you." He had done 80 before. Her husband then threat- ened her and struck her. bhe never knew when she want into the house whether eh* was to have a blow or not —The defendant said his wife had been visiting. the Salvation Army too much and neglecting her children. On Saturday night she came in at twenty-five minutes to eleven. He had bad to put up with a great deal.—Mr. Lewin (magis- trates' clerk) : Is it a fact that you attend the Salvation Army and leave your children to take care of themselves?— The complainant: No.—Mr. Evans: It is a pity that people like you cannot manage to live together quietly.—The defendant said his wife had been a member of the Army since it came to Widnes.—Mr. Evans said there was no doubt that if a married woman stopped out until nearly eleven and twelve o'clock at night attending the Salvation Army meetings, or any other meetings, it mast lead to neg- lect of her family. He thought the justice of the case would be met by the defendant paying the costs and pro- mising not to illtreat her again.—The defendant : If she will behave anything like I won't —The magistrate asked the wife if te would not stop out late at night.—The com- plainant said she was net out late ' • she was marketing on the eight in question.—The defendant There is a party in court that can prove you are in the habit of keeping out until half-past eleven—The magistrate : You had no right to strike your wife.—Defeudant : I had no decent clothes to come here in, as they are in pawn.—The magistrate : If you will promise not to strike her again and Qay 7e 61 costs the CASS will be withdravro.—The defendant, who laboured under the idea that he was justified in striking his wife under such circumstances, replied with his heal thrown defiantly back, "No, that is my final answer."—He was then hound over to keep the peace for three moeths, himself in £lO and one surety of £5, and was ordered to pay 15s ,costs.

Amongst toe accounts of the Finance Committee was an acceunt of £22 18t 61 from Mr. Lineker, the law clerk.— The Chairman said be objected to this bill, because be did not consider that the Board were entitled to pay it. One item of Et 153 61, was for an agreement with Messrs. Clolus and Co., that was to have been drawn up, and it was understood that Messrs Clolus would pay for it.. The next item had reference to Runcorn Gas C mmany and the rate- payers' meeting, the amount being £3 14a Si for work done, and done he (the chairman) believed as lair clerk to the Board. Then there was £l5 9s 21 for drawing up the night soil contract and bond.—Mr. Speakman suggested that as this matter would involve a great amount of discussion, the whole subject should be referred to a committee of the whole Board.—The Chairman agreed to this course.—The Law Clerk said after the chairman's statement it would only be fair that he should have something to say upon the matter. —Mr. Lake Don't you think the result would speak for itself one way or anoteer.—The Law Clerk said if Mr. Shaw thought that work should be done by the law clerk for 193 2t a month then he was very much mistaken.—The Chairman : That is not the point at all.—Mr. Speakman : move that the subject be referred to a committee of the whole-Board. I don't think anything is to be gained by discussing it publicly.—Mr. Pritchard eat:loaded the motion. —The Chairman was sure no member of the Board desired anything except what was perfectly right, but seeing that the members of the Board are surcharged for what is be- lieved to be an irregularity, and if the duties of the law clerk bound this particular case then the Board should not make a mistake. Whatever agreement may have been drawn up, if it did not embrace this work and was not satisfactory to both parties, then some &her arrangement should be made. —The Law Clerk stated that there bad been no objection made by the auditor to any similar account in the past. He wished the public to understand that. fie did not think he ought to be prejudiced as he was being prejudiced.— The Chairman said be did not wish to prejudice the law clerk in any way, but still the Board ought to proceed on business liners. If the duties as arranged were defective they ought to be altered. He did not wish any person con- nected with that Board not to be properly remunerated.— The motion was carried.

The minutes of the Parliamentary Committee did not contain any facts that have not been previously reported.— Mr. Like said it had been ir.timated to him that the same objections which prevented him milting any remarks about the Ship Canal Bill at a previous meeting were applicable to that day. He did not wish to run counter to the views of the committee, or to do anything that would in any way hamper the committee, as they had the conduct of the business and were best able to judge. He should still re- serve his right to enter his protest whenever he thought necessary—The Chairman : I am sorry it cannot be done to-day.—Mr. Lake replied that he was quite prepared.—Mr. Pritchard said there were negmiations going on at the pre- sent time. The committee had no objection to their con- duct being discussed if the members thought it prudent to do so. The committee did not wish the members to with- hold anything they might have to say upon the subject— they were quite prepared to discuss it.—The Chairman said the committee did not wish the public to feel that there was any question affecting what had been done that they were afraid of bringing before the Board. If the public had any impression that the committee were afraid of an in- vestigation or a discussion upon this matter, they would prefer that the impression should be removed whatever the result might be.—Mr. Speakman said negotiations of an im- patent character were proceeding, and he thought very successfully, and they ought t) be very much obliged to Mr. Lake for putting the case in the way he had. In the interests of the town, which they all represented, be thought silence NCO best at the present moment.—Mr. Grice con- fessed to a personal craving for a little more information . as to the position of the Board with regard to the Cant! ' Bill, but after Mr. Speakman's remark that negotiations ' were proceeding successfully it would, in his opinion, be wise to defer the discussion to a future meeting.—The Chairman : The matter is in the bands of the Board. I am sure the committee are prepared to give you every in- formation in their power, and allow you to raise the matter in any way you please. They simply express their opin- ion, but they are not anxious that a false impression should go to the public that they are:afraid of any fair investiga- tion.—Mr. Lake said he failed to see if the negotiations were unchanged why the ummittes should now be so anxious to have discussion, when at the last meeting they requested him not to open the subject. He did not in'end to open the discussion that morning. One reason was that a member of the deputation to whose conduct he wished more particularly to refer was uot present, and he did not think It fair to criticise his conduct in hisiabsence.

11IE NUISANCE INSPECTOR. A letter was read from the Local Government Board ap- proving of the appointment of a sanitary insp-ctor. The Chairman explained that there was a slight informality in the appointment of Mr. Percival, and the formality of ad- vertising would have to be gone through again. He had no doubt it would be the pleasure ot the Board to re-appoint the present inmector. I The Board then went into committee.

Pa. COMMERCIAL TRAVELLER IN BAD COMPANY. At Runcorn Peav Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. J. firundrit and Mr: C. Reynolds, Thrbert Dwyer, landlord of the BI UP Ball Beerhouse, WAS summoned to answer a charge ,of permitt lag drunkenness on his premises. Joseph Henry But man, commercial traveller, of Liverpool, was summoned

for being drunk on the premises.--Mr. C. El. Letin ap- peared for Dwyer. About 20 minutes past four on Friday, the 29th ult., P.C. Bryan found Bulman in the bar of the Blue Ball in a helpless state of drunkenness. There were also three women there, and all had giess(s of beer before them Hillman got hold of a glass of beer, bat the landlady *matched it from his hand, and stated that it belonged is r One of the women. Sne afterwards handed it back to Rud- man.. Subsequently P.S. Walley went in search of Bulman, and discovered him in a house iii Fryer•street, kept by a man named Oliver. There were three prostitutes in tat, room. On the table was a quart jug of beer, and four !glasses. Bulman was drunk, and the sergeant told him he was sorry to see such a respectable man in that house, as it was very likely that ha would leave with leas property than he had when be entered. Knowing the character of the house the ogicer counted Bulman's money. a task which Bulman could not do himself, and saw that hie gold watch and travelling bag were sae. . He then told the women he should hold them responsible if a robbery took place.—ln reply to Mr. Lewin, P.S. Walley said Bulman was in such a condition that the Railway Company would not convey him to Liverpool, and he had to stay at Wilson's Hotel all night. In the room he saw Bulmen attonpt to give one of the women a kiss, cad be fell backwards in a corner.—Mm. Dwyer deposed that Batman called at the Blue Ball .to eolicit an order for glasses and cigars for the = firm for which he travelled. The glass 'he took hold of I belonged to a woman. One of the glasses had been left by : a person who had gone ant. Bulman said he would treat the women to a drink, but he went out without paying. He was never supplied with liquor. —The defendant Dwyer said 'he did not consider the man drunk when he saw him, and `Grace Walker also stated that he was " qu,te eober."—Jane Oliver, a married woman, said she first met Bialman at the top of Fryer-street in the morning, when he raid " good morning, Jane." She and another woman went to several public-houses with him. In the afternoon she and ether two women went whh him to the Blue Ball. She carried his bag because he said he felt tired and lazy. He called for three glasses of beer for them, but he had none himself, and he did not pay. In her house he sent for three or four quarts of ale, and when he left was able to carry his bag and umbrella—Annie Marshall said Bulman had'nothing to drink in the Blue Bal'.—Thomas Lea, grocer, Church,- streerrstated he saw Bulman going along with two women, and as he had had some drink, and was not in safe company, ' he told, a constable.—DAendant Buhl:lan was called,, and denied that he was supplied with drink at the Blue Ball.— The Chairman said there was no doubt in tle• case, and Dwyer would be fined 20s and les ad costs; iu default, a month's imprisonment. He thought that it was unnecessary to say anything to Bulman after the evidence that had been given. They regretted to see a man in his position in Buell disgrace and in such company, and they hoped it weuld be a lessen to him for the future. He would be fined sean4 costs.—Bulman appeared to feel his position acutely.

GREAT SANKEY SCHOOL BOARD.—A meeting of this body was held at the Boardroom at Great San- key, on Tuesday afternoon when the chair was oc- cupied by Mr. J. Turner, ;here being also present. Messrs. W. B. Kerfoot (vice-chairman), J. C. Ridg- way, John Cook, and S. Sutton (clerk.)—The Clerk read an agreement drawn up between William Dampier Jeans, Warrington, solicitor, and the Board, to sell 3,673 square yards of land at Sankey, to the Board, for £460, the purchasers to fence off the southerly and westerly sides with a temporary fence, to keep cattle from trespassing, and as soon as practicable to fence off the same with a good, substantial brick wall at a sufficient height to pre- vent children from trespassing on adjacent land. In the event of a street being laid out west of the site the purchasers to bear one half of the expense of making it. After a short discussion the agree-. ment was approved and the seal of the Board was ordered to be affixed to it.—lt was resolved to bor- row, for the purchase of land, and building schools, Itc., the sum of £2,500 from Messrs. Jersey and Preston, to be repaid in 50 years at equal half- yearly instalments of principal and interest com- bined, and the clerk was instructed to obtain the sanction of the Education Department to the proposed loan,—This was the Whole of the busi- ness.

POLICE INTELLIGENCE
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

BArnlDAY—Before Aldermen Burgess and Ct. anthey. BILSCELLANEOI79.—AMbrOe 0 Foden, 72, Cockhedge-lane, was charged with neglecting to maintain his family. He was ordered to pay the costs of the case and discharged on promising to abstain from drink.—James Connolly, charged with begging in Church •street on the previous evening, was discharged on promisimr to leave the town. MoNDAY—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Coun- ... . .

, cillor Greening, and Mr. J. Fairclough. MISCELLANEOUS —The following cases of drunkenness were dealt with :—Jane Runcarn in Lyme-street, on the adth nit, sent to prison for 14 days; Nolan (65th appear- ance), in Buttermarket-street, on the 30th ult., fined 103 and costs ' • Ellis McGrabb, in Hill-street, on the 30th ult., fined 5s ; Eliz..beth Boschurch, in Buttermarket-street, on , the 31st ult., sent to Walton for a month ' • Catherine Woods, in Silver-street, on the 23rd ult., fined 5. and costs ; Maria Brett, in Bridge-st., on the 25th ult. fined 53 and costs; similar fines were imposed on Bridget Oly. Charles Daniel, and Ed- ward Boylry for drunkenness.--Michael McDonald and a man named Colman were charged with fighting in Winwick- street on the 25 h ult., and were bound over to be of good behaviour.--Michael Connor, a boy, who was charged with playing " peggy " in Mersey-street, on the 27th ult., was cautioned and dismissed.--John Backbonse, for being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart and furiously driving the same in Buttermarket-street on the 25th ult was, on the evidence of P.C. Baxendale, fined 5s and costa for each offence.—John Thomas Miller, for playing pitch and toss on the LA M y, at Artdey, was ordered to pay the costs ; and a fine of 2, di each was imposed on Thomas O'Brien and Samuel Whitehouse for a similar offence, com- mitted on the 24th May; Three young men named Quinn, Rooney, and Ward were similarly chewed, and the case was adjourned for a week, as they denied the offence.--John Gibbons, charged with begging at Latchford on the let inst., was dismissed on pro nising to leave the town.-- Joseph McDonald and Henry Barton were each fined is for wheeling barrows en the pavement.--Henry Ball and a person named C.:,ney were each fiaed Is for allowing the chimneys of their houses to boon fire.—Four boys named Horton, Southern, Timmins, and fthealey were charged with stone throwing on the 23rd ult. Southern, who has been before the court on another occasion, was fined ss, and the other defendants were each fined 2i 6d. ALLEGED TintFr.—Mary Ann Wood was charged with stealing a shawl on the 23rd ult., at Salford, and with failing to report herself to the police. She was ordered to be handed over to the Salford police. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASES.—The following parents were summoned by Mr. Li. Riley, scheol attendance officer, for non-compliance with the Education Act :—Charles Higgin- son, labourer, Stamford-street. In this case Mr. Riley said defendant was brought before the magistrates recently, and the magistrates stated that if be came before them again the bey would be sent to the ship " Clio." It, however, came out that the ship was full, and the magistrates, tak- ing into consideration the fact that the boy was to be blamed in the matter, ordered him to receive 12 strokes with the birch rod.—Alfred Cooke, tanner, of Latchford; Peter Kelly, labourer, Foundry-street; S imuel Whitehouse, railway man, Fennell-street ; James Tickle, Nicholson-street ; and John Rafferty, forgemsn, Friars'-green, were each fined Sc ; and Thomas Caldwell and William Todd were fined lOs each, there being two cases against each of the defendants.—ln the case of Ann Leech, an order was made for the children to be admitted into the Workhouse, the mother being in a state of poverty. Trmanes—Before Alderman Chandley. .

MISCELLANEOUS.—Sarah Ellen Wilkinson ;sae sent to prison for 14 days for beieg drunk and disorderly on the previous evening; and two militiamen named Charles Oliver and Thomas Helley were ordered to be banded over to the authorities, they being charged with being drank and die- gderly in Bridge-street on the previous evening. WEDNISDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclongh. DunstoluiLls•—tsllen McCarthy, for Wing drunk and disorderly in Parcivarslard on the previous eveuipg, was fined fis and coats, or seven flap' imprisonment. THURSDAY.—Befori Major Litton. MISCELLANEOUS.—Janothan Brown, 'a cripple, charged with drunkenness in Buttermarket-street, on the .previous evening, was dismissed on promising io leave tne ..----EdWard Webb, charged with being drunk in Bewsey- road the previous evening, was dismissed.--Walter Sykes was sent to prison for seven days for sleeping in a shed at Bank Park. FElDay.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and

Captain Reynolds. MISCELLAYEOI79.—EIizabeth Eisthana and a girl named Conway were each fined 5s and costs for drunkenness Sarah Bell, of the Old Crow Inn, was piimmoned for serving liquor during prohioited hours, and Ann Cunliffe for being en the premises. Cunliffe Went to the house with some friends who were travellers, and produced their rail- way tickets. The Bench dismissed both cases on payment, of ceets.—Edward Thomas was summoned by Mr. Shearer, school attendance officer, for not sending his child to school. An attendance order was granted.—Ellen Hughes was sum- moned by Sarah Quinn for assaulting her on the let inst. The case was adjourned.—Catherine Robinson, for Psatilt- jag Nary Ireland, was bound over to keep the peace. Fan PRETENCES.—Marpret Ford, a married woman, was charged with obtaining relief from the Guardians of the Poor by making a false statement. She said •that she had three children, whereas she had only two, a,pd by that means obtained more relief. The case fell tbrough in con- sequence of a technicality, the sumniOns not having been taken out while she was in receipt of relief.

WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAS.—Betore Mr. Ed. Greenall and Mr. J. Marson, MISCELLANBOUS.—Patrick McDonald, charged with being drank and disorderly on the 13th ult, was tined 10s and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment.—Harold Ball was charged with having his horse on the footpath at Poulton on the 24th ult. He WAS order‘d to pay 7,1 61 and costs.—Wm. McMillan, for riding upon a cart at Woolston whilst asleep, on the 29th ult, was acted is and costs.—Joseph Pilling, for allowing two horses to stray en the highway, at Winwick- road, on the 31st nit, was fined 5a and costs.—Jobn Evans and Daniel Allen were charged, the former with being at too far a distance from a cart of which be was in charge, at Great Sankey, on the 24th nit, and the latter with being asleep whilst in charge at the same time and place. They were each ordered to pay 2a 61 and coats.

div.head: RUNCORN PET FY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. Charles
div.p: RUNCORN PET FY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. Charles

Reynolds. UNREGISTERED LODGING HOUSES.—Sarah Clarkson, of Wilson's-row, was summoned for keeping an unregistered lodging-house. The defendant, who had been previously convicted of a similar offeace, was fined £2 and coats £l. Mary Wilson, of Jackson's-lane, was summoned for a like offence, and was fined 103 and costs. Mr. W. H. Linaker prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Commissioners, and the cases were proved by Mr. Percival, nuisance in-

Spector. tee DOG LICENSES WANTED.—Philip Taylor, of Sutton, and Thomas Molyneux were each fined 5s and costs for keeping a dog without license. 800 wn OVER.—WM Evans, a young 'fellow, was charged with using threatening language towards Mary Haddock, an old woman, living in Sewell-street The d?- fandant was bound over to keep the peace for six months in his own recognisances of £5, and pay the costa 7s 61. Rebecca Bazley and Sarah Clark, for fighting in Haltri- road, and Edward Hankinson and James Jones for fighting on the fair ground, were each dealt with in a similar manner. ASSICLTS BY Woucx —Amanda Smith, of Wdlington- street, was summoned by Thomas Forshaw for an assault. The evidence showed that Forshaw lived in the same house as Smith, and cohabited with her husband's sister. On the' evening of the 16th May an argnment arose as to the ownership of a Bible, and the defendant struck the com- plainant on the side with a poker, and would certainly have injured him had the weapon not ku!en forcibly taken from her. The defendant, who denied using the poker, was fined 103 and costs 111 63, or in default 14 days.—Ada Evans was summoned for assaulting Mary Evans on the 2ith ult. While in the street some words passed between the women, with the result that Ada struck Mary on the face. A fine of 5s and costs was imposed. DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence George Hayes, Eliza Fearneth, John Kelly, Martin Griffiths, and John Burke were each fined.
