NOTES BY THE WAY. After Kent had defeated Yorkshire in the early part of last week, great importance was attached to their encounter with Lancashire at Old Trail .)rd. Many Lancastrians were doubtful about the result, and, but for the performances of Briggs, Crossland, and Mr. Kershaw, they would un- doubtedly have cut up very badly. Thu most interesting feature of the whole game was the splendid performance of Briggs. His first innings of 58 was a good one, though he was missed by Lord Harris before he had broken his "duck." His second innings was a still better performance, and is to be classed as one of the finest exhibitions seen at Old Traff for a ling time back. Ibe captain's 61 were put with dash, but with the exception of Briggs, the finest play was shown by Mr. Roper and Barlow. Crossland, on Thursday, in his second over bowled Lord Harris, but Lis lordship had his revenge next day by cutting off the pro very short with a neat catch. In their second innings Kent played up well. Mr Jones batted well, but he was missed by both Briggs and Crossland. The last wicket added no fewer than 27 runs, but at the conclusion the 85u1h2r0er5 were 42 funs behind. At the beginning of the season Kent's prospects were generally voted anything but promising, but up to the pre-

div.head: EXAAIINER..SATURDAY, ,JUNE 6, 1885.
div.p: THE EXAAIINER..SATURDAY, ,JUNE 6, 1885.

rent their performances have been good. The most note- worthy was their victory over Yorkshire. This was un- doubtedly owing in a great measure, as indeed, are the lwho!e of the resul-s so far, to the excellent form of the i brothers H-.arne. Gorge and Frank are both in Rood bat• ' ting form, but the youngest son of the Catford Bridge cus- todian has proved himself one of the most dangerous slow bowlers of the day. In the second innings of Yorkshire, none except Louis Hall were able to play him, and during the whole match 13 wickets fell to him for•4B runs.

A weak team had been got together by the gentlemen of England to meet the Oxford University. The gentlemen were captained by Mr. A J. Webbe, and, with the exception of Messrs. &mid, Robertson, and Rotherham, the team was composed entirely of Oxfo d men. fhe match was produc- tive of satne good play, the Gentlemen winning easily by sewn wickets.

At Oxford and Cambridge cricket is still very freely en- gaged in, and the chances of the teams in the inter-Univer- sity match are daily becoming more easily ascertain- able. At pre•ent the Oxford men are the favourites, but the game will by DO me ins be a one-sided one. Cambridge has just had a severe lesson taught them by Yorkshire, and Oxford has been similarly treated by the Gentlemen of Eng- land.
Inspector Spinks proved taking Clarke to Mr. Davies' office, where he made an affidavit. No thmats whatever were made to Clarke.

Mr. William Mu! lard, clerk to the Official Receiver, said that on the fish of March he locked Spann's premises up, and took possession of the keys. The premises were locked up on the night of the 17th March. Elizabeth Clarke, wife of John Clarke, and mother of Nathaniel Clarke, was the first witness called by Mr. Walton. She denied what was stated in Chapman's affidavit with reference to her receiving tools from him. (Chapman.).

• . - John Clarke said be kept the Royal Oak Branch, James- street. Chapman never brought any tools to him. His son brought some tools home, but witness ordered him to take them back. They were only in the house one night.— Cross-examined by Mr. Davies : He ordered his son to take the tools back because he flu heard there was something wrong.

Mr. Joseph Ashton, Bridge Inn, Latchford, said there were scme things sent to his house from Spann's about the beginning of March. One of the things was a waggonette which belonged to witness. There were some other things sent down at the same time. He ordered them to be taken back at once, as they did not belong to him.—Cross-ex- amined by Mr. Davies: ,lie saw some ironwork amongst the things. _
The order to annul the composition was made, aad Spann was re-adjudicated a bankrupt.

div.head: IMPORTANT_BANKRqTCY CASE.
div.p: IMPORTANT_BANKRqTCY CASE.

STRANGE DISCLOSURES. At Warrington County Court on Monday, before hi Honour Judge Ffoulkes, an application was made by Mr. P. Davies, solicitor, acting on behalf of Mr. Garland, iron- monger, Bridge-street, a creditor of the estate of Richard Spann, wheelwright, Friare-greel, to annul an order of composition in the matter of Spann, and adjudicate him a bankrupt. Mr. Ridgway watched the case as official re- ceiver, and Mr. Walton, barrister, Liverpool (instructed by Mr. A. Browne, solicitor), opposed the applieation on behalf of Spann.—Mr. Davies said that he made his application under sub-section 11 ot section 18 of the Bankruptcy Act, 1883. Mr. Garland, his client, was a creditor for the sum of £3445, and on the 21st February, 1885, he took out a writ against Richard Spann, and he proved on the estate for the amount altogether of £35 18e op. An appearance was entered to the writ on the 2tstti of the same month. Oa the following sth March the debtor filed his petition. Mr. Garland, being the only creditor to a large amount in Warrington, and having an idea that Spann was not a man who should have flied his petition, made certain inquiries, which were not of such a nature that he could make use of them at the public exam- ination of the debtor. He believed that the official receiver did all that he could under the circumstances to try and ferret out the matter before the public examination. His Honour no doubt would be well aware as to how the bank- rupt answered the questions that were put to him by the official receiver and on behalf of Mr. Garland. In the answering of the questions the bankrupt stated that he kept no books except some few that be mentioned, and he aloe said that nothing had been removed and that his state:nem of affairs was a true one. During the course of the proceed- ings James Ctiapman, who was a foreman wheelwright, and a man named Bridge, came voluntarily to Mr. Gayland and made Statements to him that he reduced to writing and were signed by the men. Mr. Garland then instructed him (Mr. Davies) to act in the matter, get a proper affidavit, and to make the ex parte application made on the previoue Thurs- day before his Honour. The first w.tuess he should call would be Mr. Garland, who would speak to having taken out the writ and afterwards instituted those proceedings. The next would be James Chapman, and if what he stated were true he should ask his Honour to grant the order, be- cause the approval of the court, which was for Spann's protection, was obtained by fraud. Chapman said that he had been for four years in the employ of Spann, who fled his petition' on the sth March. On the previous Tuesday, the 3rd March, he, along with Bridge, seemed to have had instructions to dispose of a great quantity of the goods a the bankrupt and distribute them in different parts of the town. If that were proved he should submit I that the statement of affairs was untrue, and that would be a traced against the creditors and certainly a fraud upon the , court. He said that he got his instructions on the 3rd I March, along with Bridge, and that he disposed of certain Portions of his property to Mr. Cross, another part to Joseph Ashton, and another to a Mr. Clarke. On the 17th March Chapman received a note saying that he must go at once to Spann's, to see him on particular business. Chapman went, and Spann, when they were in the paint-room said that they, referring to the official receiver or his officers' had been trying to find something that he had hidden, and that he was afraid they would make another search, and there- fore he wanted to remove what he had written. Spann then showed- him a place where were a large quantity f var- nishes; paints, ironwork, and other things, which Chapman put down at the value of £5O. Chapman could not tell where all these things were placed, but he saw Spann tak- ing something burning, which he described as parts of books and papers, from the fire and putting them in a raintub. Afterwards Spann told the apprentice to take the papers out and burn them again. On the following day Spann denied that he ever kept any time books, except what had been produced to the official receiver. Spann put down the value of his assets at a considerable amount less than the valua- tion afterwards made by Mr. Sutton, and if what Chapman said were true Mr. Sutton should have valued many other things, and, had all been included, he thought it was very likely that the assets would have paid 20s iii the £ instead of 4% Evidence was then called. Joseph Smith Garland, ironmonger, Bridge-street, War- rington, gave evidence bearing out the opening statement of Mr. Davies, and said that Chapman ars' Bridge made a statement to him and signed a paper reading, "We the undersigned, certify that at Richard Spann's instructions we removed on March 3rd the articles enumerated on list at- tached, the former part to Mr. John Cross, Rose and Crown- street, the second lot to Mr. Ashton% Bridge Inn, and the third part to Mr. John Clarke, Oak Branch. Latchford. James Chapman, wheelwright, formerly employed by Spann, and now living at Nantwich, said that to the best of his knowledge the affidavit he had made was true. In answer to Mr. Walton, witness said be did not vrish to im- port a feeling into the case that ought not to exist. He was examined by Mr. Walton as to several letters he had written to Spann. In one of them he said that he was surprised at Spann's mean and cowardly conduct to- wards him, and he now (13th May) gave him fair warning that unless he gave up all the tools, or the pawn tickets for the same, together with the piper he had sent in respect of them before four o'clock that day, and sent the same to him, together with one sovereign for lose of time and anxiety he had to suffer in consequence of his barefaced roguery, he should inform Mr. Davies and Mr. Garland that he and Bridge had removed the enclosed list of goods to certain places by his instructions, as Spann's servants, twe days previous to the filing of the petition, and that be had not valued or accounted to his creditors for such said property, which he valued at £3O, and that he had, there- fore, defrauded his creditors out of the real value of his estate. Chapman, in the last part of his letter, used some very strong language with reference to Spann. Mr. Walton: You had pawned the tools, and you could not afford to get them out? I pawned them, being out of work. —And Spann was to get them out—to advance sufficient to get them from the pawnshops? On a promise that I was to work for him.—When did you pawn the tools? Some time before, was it not? Yes.—How long before? Some two years before, and some about, perhaps, two months ago.— Were they not Spann's tonle No, Heye they got Spann's name en? No, not unless he has put it on, which he is quite capable of doing.—l thought you did not want to import feeling into the case? I don't wish to import, I wish to export as much as I can. (Laughter.)—What you demanded in this letter was this piece of paper and the tools, or the pawntickets and a sovereign? Yes.—What was the sovereign for? For loss of time and anxiety.—lf you got what von wanted from Spann you undertook to leave the town? Yes, and his dirty business with him.— If you did not get the sovereign and these things he was to pay the penalty? Yes. That is correctly my meaning.— His Honour : What was the penalty? That I would expose him and inform Mr. Garland.—Mr. Walton: That you would tell the story which is in the affidavit? Yes. Mr. Walton read another letter from Chapman to Spann, in which he said, under date 18th May, "This is the third and last warning. I have, as you know, been thrown on the , streets without food, or work, or tools to work with, and you have under a false and lying pretence obtained posses- sion of my tools, and also branded me as a thief, and now, driven to the last extremity, I must pay you back in your own base coin; but if you will, as soon as you read this, send to me the bass of my own tools I pawned for 12s, and gave you the ticket to redeem as you promised, or give me back the ticket, and in addition to that send me a few ebil- I inge for railway fares forms and wife, we will instantly leave the town to work elsewhere, as you will in a few hours learn that it will be the only thing you can do to benefit yourself and family. It should not be a question of shillings or pounds. Had you c mplied with my previous letters you would have been out of danger, and if you per- sist in refusing my rights your ruin is complete, but if I instantly go away far enough you will be saved: I had 30 minutes' interview with Cbales Bradlaugh—(laughter)-- on Saturday afternoon, at the Patten Arms Hotel, and he has advised me on the whole question. I wait for an almost immediate reply, say not later than eight o'clock this (Monday) morning, and certainly I shall not see,,you. Send one of the lads up." To these letters Spann replied, stating that he did not intend to have money extorted from him in any such manner. and that if he (Chapman) knew of any goods belonging to the estate he must at once tell him where they were. He had never given any instructions to any one to remove his goods previous to his liquidation. If. Spann added, Chapman had any information t) impart with respect to his affairs, let him know at once, as he was prepared to go with him to investigate the matter or have the estate re-valued: Spann, on the 18th May, wrote again to Chapman, in which he said :—"Sir,—ln reply to yours of this morning, I may tell you that you have branded yourself a thief by pawning my goods without my permission; but now as you have made so many allegations about me, and you choose to carry the matter further, you had better get another 30 minutes' interview with C.B.—(laughter)—and tell him all about it truthfully, and he will advise you." (Laughter.) I Spann added that "ho was prepared to defend himself before any tabunal.”—Witneas was further examined by Mr. Walton with reference to his affidavits and the removal of certain goods. David Rankin, manager for Messrs. Scales and Salter, Bridge-street, creditors for an amount of 155., spoke to sea ing Chapman and two other men taking a truck load of timber down Bridge-street on the morning of the day en which Spann filed his petition. Nathaniel Clarke, Royal Oak Branch, Latchford, appren- tice te Spann, said that on the 17th March he went to Spann's house' at about nine or -ten o'clock at night. Spann sent for him. When he got there Spann said he had heard a rumour that there was something under the paint-room floor. Spann field him to get a I edder to get' Into the store-room, go to the paint-room, and unbolt the door. He did this by taking screws off the store-room lock. Two planks were taken up, and a quantity of bolts, screws, springs, and paints were taken from under the floor. He left the house at 630 in the morning. He saw Spann take I something out of the fite wflich looked like soot and I papers. In the morning he collected the papers out of the yard and pot them in the fire. He did that by Spann's instructions. On the 4th of March he took Spann's bass Of tools to his (witness) house, but his father would not let : them' remain there, and he took them back to Spann on [ the day the petition was filed. P.C. Baxeedale said that on the 17th March he saw spark's flying from Spann's chimney. Seeing a light in the house he knocked at the door, and be was immediately , answered by Spann. Witness told Spann he would have , the chimney on fire if he were not careful, to which'Spann replied that he was expecting a cow to calve—(laughter)— and was drawing up the fire in Order to get a pan of boiling water. The fire was instantly put out.

div.head: BURGLARY NEAR WARRINGTON.
div.p: BURGLARY NEAR WARRINGTON.

At an Occasional Court held before Mr. James Matson, at the ofiice of Messrs. Nicholson, White, and Nicholson, Bank-street, Warrington, on Wednesday, a rough-looking man named George Corbett, who stated that he came from , Northwich, was charged with committing a burglary at the 4 house of Mr. John Edmund Davies, actuary of the Warring- ton Savings Bank, who resides at Appleton, Cheshire.—Mr. Davies said that on the previous night he did not examine , the windows or fastenings of his house, but he looked to see th,t the front and back doors were fastened. In one of the ; windows in the front room of the ground floor, which was used as a nursery, there were two small panes of glass, which had -beeu broken for some time. The space of the two windows, however, was only six by three inches. He had examined the window that morning, and thought it , possible for a person to put his hand in through the opening, land undo the catch inside. At about seven o'clock, in con- sequence of what he was told by one of the servants, he examined the nursery, in company with Sergeant Booth, and feuod that a robbery had been committed there and in other parts of the house during the night. Tke windows were closed, and in the stale condition as he sew them on the previous night. A quantity of wearing apparel had been taken from the house, including the cloth that was on the nursery table the nieht before, his wife's fur cloak, his brier pipe a copper kettle, five pairs of boots, and a quantity of clothing belonging to Mrs. Davies, the cebdren, and the servants. That morning he saw the various articles now produced, at the Stockton Heath police etatior., and identified some of them as his property. He believed all the articles to be big property, and that of the servants, but was not able to identify all. Some were marked with his name.—lsabella Mary Barnard, , nurse, in the employ of Mr. Davies, said that she was in the nursery at nine o'cleck the previous night. It was a front room on the ground floor, and had a small bay win- dow. The window was shut. She was not sure whether it was fastened on the previous evening. When she came down stairs in the morning she found that a number of articles bad been taken from the room and other parts of the premises. The articles produced she identified as being the property of Mr. Davies with the exception of what be- longed to the servants.—John Broady, gamekeeper to Mr. T. 11. Lyon, of Appleton, stated that about four o'clock that morning he was in a wood in the -neighbourhood of Hill Cliff when he met the prisoner carrying a bag. Witness asked him what he was doing there, and prisoner replied that he was going to Runcorn. He also siid he was from Northwich, was a stranger, was drunk on the previous night and Lad lost his way. Witnese sale he should take him to the police. station, Ye. ereupon prisoner asked him not, saying that he was a buyer of clothes, and through being drunk had lost his license, and would g,t into trouPle if he were given into the hands of the police. Witness saw same of the articles in the bag and insisted on taking prisoner to the police station. , On the way prisoner said to him "You will be old yourself some day, and y :u will get a bullet in you like the rest."— , P.C. Mellor, 186, Cheshire police, stationed at Stretton, proved receiving the prisoner from the custody of the lastl , witness at shout 530 that morning. In answer to questions, prisoner admitted having taken the articles from the house of Mr. Davies.—S,rgeant Booth, Stockton Heath, deposed to searching the prisoner, in whose posseesion he found three knives, a wax candle, a quantity of safety matches, and a small purse containing is 41. He afterwards examined the window of Mr. Davies' house, and found appearances of its having been forcibly entered. On the application of the seageant prisoner was remanded to the following morn- ing.—Prisoner was again brought up on Thursday morning, when, further evidence having been given, he was commit- ted for trial.

div.head: COLLIERY DISASTER IN DURHAM.
div.p: COLLIERY DISASTER IN DURHAM.

SERIOUS LOSS OF LIFE. An accident of a terrible character occurred at noon on 'Wednesday at the Margaret Pit, Philadelphia, one of the group of the Lembton collieries owned by Lord Durham. Hitherto the colliery has enjoyed immunity from accidents of a disastrous character. It seems that the pit, which is 115 fathoms in depth, is worked by au ordinary shaft. There are four seams, named the Five-quarter, Main Caal, the Maudlin, and the Hutton. At the time of the accident there were some hundreds of men and boys in the pit. Of this nuetber twenty-five or twenty-six were working in what is crlled the New Maudlin seam. Whilst cutting through s•me stone some old works were tapped, and there was an inrush of water and gas. An alarm was at once raised, and Mae in the other workings made their way to the bottom of the shaft. There 193, no denaage done to the shaft, and as the ventilation continued good the ztent of the disaster was soon ascertained. Mr. Listimae, the manager, and Tate, son of the resident viewer, quickly descended the mine along with an ex- ploring party, and it then became known that some 25 or 26 men and boys were entombed in the New Maudlin seam. , The remainder of the miners who had made their way to the he torn of the Elhaft were Atli to the hank, and every effort I possible waft made to rescue the unfortunate men. Mean- while exaggerated reports which had been circulated caused the eit mouth to be speedily thronged with masses of men, women, and children, but throughout the day there were no unusual or heartrending scenes. About four o'clock two of the entombed were rescued. Their names were Rennison Carter, buck overman an& putter, end a boy named Ains- worth. They were both extremely exhausted on reaching the surface, and Carter died shortly afterwards, He leaves a widow and seven children. Ainsworth was attended by' ' the medical gentlemen present, and quickly came round, and subsequently said that about dinner time he heard a rush like water, and went to see what it was, and met Carter, the back overman. Carter was very much exhausted, and fell down, and Ainsworth tried to raise him. In endeavouring to raise him he was overcome, and remembered nothing more till he was rescued. About five o'clock Mr. Tate came to bank, and Mr. Patterson, of the Durham Miners' Association, in charge of a relief party, descended the mine. Mr. Tate reported that the air cerrents were right, I and that they had communicated with 13 of the entombed met', who had answered that they were all right. Some of the 13 had already been rescued, and would be speedily Bent to bank. There were still seven or eight that they had been unable to communicate with, but from the fact that 13 were all right it was a hopeful sign they might still be alive. About a quarter to six o'clock a putter lad named Middlemae was rescued and sent to bank, and was quickly followed by two brothers named Daglish. All three were more or less exhausted, but were still able to walk home. About seven o'clock on Wednesday evening the explorers came upon a batch of twelve of the imprisoned miners. These men had been driven into the spet only partially fimcled, but the air was so foul that it was evident they could not live long in it. One of them suggested breaking through a . wooden partition separating the air courdes or sections in the pit. This was partially effected, and they soon become conscious of an improvement in the atmosphere. After being confined for seven hours they beard the sound of the approaching rescuing party and succeeded in giving juror- mation of their poaition. When extricated they were in a terribly exhausted condition. There are still 12 men in the pit, and faint hopes are entertained of saving them. The men have appointed local inspectors under the Mines' Regulation Act. The Press Assm'ation's correspondent, telegraphing from Fencehouses at eight o'clock on Thursday morning, said affairs at the Peggy Pit remained the same. The explorers who went down the pit had come to the bank and reported the water to be subsided. Precautions were taken by strengthening the timbering of the roof to prevent accidents to the explorers. A report from the Margaret Pit fence houses states that the water his been reduced, hut the sweep of water through the drifts had carried away supports, and heavy falls have occurred which make it doubtful when the place where the twelve men are imprisoned will be reached. Mr. Atkinson, Government Inspector, who left the mine at five o'clock on Thursdity, states that he was within 15 yards of the spot, but could get no sound in reply to his communications. It , is feared that 12 men have perished. On Thursday, an inquest was opened at Dewbattle upon Rennison Carter, deputy, who died on Wednesday from in- haling noxious gas at the Peggy Pit. Only evidence of identification was called, and after the coroner had sugges- ted the advisalility of postponing the inquiry until more bodies should be rocovered if those in the pit are dead, the irquest wae adjourned.
Mr. J. H. Crro•field haa accepted the invitation to stand as the Liboral candidate for the Gorton Division of South- east Lancashire.

STREET STABBING —At Cambridge, on Monday, three Itilian musiciane were charged with having stabbed several persons with knives in the streets of the town. on Sunday evening. Eight pers.ns, it was ststed, had been wounded by the prisoners, one haring sustlined serious injuries. The sc- cused were said to have entered a public-house in one in- stance and attacked the occupants indiscriminately. They were remsnied for a week. ANGELS' CAICFS (Patented). div.head: NEW BOOKS, &c,
div.p: NEW BOOKS, &c,

The "Speeches of Jacob Bright, M.P., 1869 to 1884" (A. Ireland and Co., Manchester), edited by Mrs Bright, form a respectable volume, and are issued in a handsome form. Mrs Bright seems to have had some difficulty in inducing her husband to consent to their reproduction, his observation being that "nobody cares to read old speeches ; " but the result justifies Mrs Bright's estimate of their value. They embrace a large number of topics— general politics being of course the staple article. There are several on Ireland and the education question, and four on the Manchester Ship Canal, besides some half dozen Parliamentary speeches. They all display clearness of statement, intelligent observation, and a logical regard of the thread of , principle which runs through things. Mr. Jacob Bright is over-shadowed as an orator by his world- famous brother" The Tribune of the People ; " but he has merits of his own which none can fail to discover who read his speeches. The volume is well worth preserving as a work of reference in- political topics. The Case for Disestablishment " is a most valu- able handbook issued by the Liberation Society. As it is published in a cheap forth (1s), no one need be without it who wants to have by him a reliable statement of the facts and arguments in'support of the claim for religious equality. The question is dealt with on every side—historical, legal, political and religious; whilst there is a copious index which makes the work all the more nseful for reference. The case is so welbraade out that, as it seems to us, there is no withstanding it, We commend the handbook to Churchmen who are looking for a way out of bondage. Cassell's Magazine for June is, as usual, bright and interesting. The serial tales are making good headway, and the finished stories are up to the average. The scientifically disposed are treated to papers on " Dr. Schilemann's Discoveries at Tiryns " and" What the Sun is made of." There are besides articles on " The Garden in June," "Hay Asthma," "Flemish Lace and Lace Makers," "A Glimpse of - New York," &c. The new prize competitionh for 1885 are announced in this issue. "The Quiver" has for frontispiece a nice picture of a nice old lady, and it is otherwise well illustrated. Photography is lend- ing its aid in giving greater detail to engraving. The Dean of Canterbury, one of the revisers, con- tributes an important article on "The Revised Ver- sion of the Old Testament," and there are several other well-written papers on kindred subjects. The "Short Arrows" are pointed and hit the mark. The twenty-first volume of "Little Folks," which has been such a great success,' closes with the present number; but there is promise of no end of good things for the future. Cassell's fine art edition of the works of Longfel- low, with its wealth of illustration, reaches part 10. The Story of Hiawatha is concluded, and we have the first part of the Courtship of Miles Standish. In the picture of Priscella, the artist has caught the right expression; there is something of archness in the face as well as gentleness and beauty. Part 17 of the Encylopcedic Dictionary continues the letter C, the meaning of every word of importance being defined by numerous quotations. For instance, a column is devoted to the word "closure," including a sketch of what is understood by it as a parlia- mentary rule. "Popular Gardening" continues the article on Propogation ; and there are valuable papers, suitably illustrated, on ferns, orchids, rose culture, glass structures, manuring, &c. The cur- rent issue of the Book of Health deals with the ap- portioningof foods, and the influence of exercise. A dietary is given, which, whilst safe as to use, ' leaves no lack of variety. Under exercise, there are statistics which dispose of some points which have 'often been under dispute. The effects of walking, limning, jumping, riding, dancing, and skating are _fully considered, and some very useful hints are , given. Part 8 of "Recent British Battles" (Cassell's) car- ' ries the reader to the close of the Transvaal War— of which with sketches, maps, and portraits he gets a very vivid picture; and we have the beginning of , the first chapter of the Egyptian War. In this con- nection we may note the new work on Egypt by I Professor G. Ebers which Messrs Cassell are issuing. It will appear in monthly parts of one shilling each, and, judging from the specimen which is before us, it will be unrivalled. There is a splendid coloured map Jvith the first number of Egypt and the Sou- dan, and altogether some 800 original illustrations are promised, which are in themselves works of art. Paper, type, and size (royal) all combine to make a magnificent work. "The Child's Own Coloured Picture Paper,"—a new and promising venture—claims to be "the first paper ever printed in chromo lithography." It is edited by Mrs E. Del; it is very bright and clever, and is sure to please the little ones. The publishers, Messrs. Dean and Son, London, obtained the gold medal for coloured toy books. "The Child's Pictorial," also coloured, is also a new undertaking. It is issued by the "Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge," and will be a monthly at twopence. An excellent start is made in the first number, pictures and 'text being alike first class.

"The Pictures of 1885 and the Men who Paint Them," a sixpenny "extra" of the "Pall Mall , Gazette," is a marvel for the money. The portraits of our great artists are exceedingly good, and the Same may be said of the reproductions of their pig- , tures, while the interviews and personal sketches I furnish just what the public like to know about ' celebrities. Ward and Lock's Technical Journal maintains its high level. Part 7 includes articles (illustrated) on ' road-making, steel-making, farming, ship-building, calico-printing, brick-laying, &c., with technical news, facts, figures, and correspondence. "The Season" and "Le Moniteur de la Mode"— the noted fashion journals—are profusely illus- trated with styles for the summer season. The col- oured plates leave nothing to be desired, and there are descriptions of novelty upon novelty in the way of costume. We have also to hand those other popular publications of the same class—" Myra's Journal of Dress and Fashion" and " Myra's Three- penny Journal." "The English Illustrated Magazine" for June is particularly strong. "In the New Forest" Is adorned with a number of fine engravings of beautiful drawings by Mr. Arthur Leomen. The London Ragamuffin " is a most readable article by Dorothy Tennant, who has very cleverly illustrated her own text. Other papers and stories are full of , interest.

div.head: SOAP CASE.
div.p: THE SOAP CASE.

The case of Lever v. flazlehurst, a motion for an injunction to restrain the defendants from so imitat- ing the plaintiff's parcels of soap so as to deceive pur- chasers, having been part heard on the last day of the sitting before the Whitsuntide vacation, was placed at the head of Tuesday's paper in the High Court of Justice, Chancery Division (before Mr. Jus- tice Chitty). When it was called on, Mr. Romer, Q.C., with whom was Mr. John Cutler, proceeded with his statement of the plaintiff's case. Mr. Romer, having alluded to his former arguments, sub. , Mittedtbat their were ether facts which showed more conclusively that the object of the defendants had not been fair trade competition, but to improperly pass off their soap as that of the plaintiffs. On the wrapper of the plaintiff's soap were the words " Sunlight Self-Washer." On the defendants' 1 wrappers was a picture of the sun in full blaze, with the words " Genuine Sun" on each side. They did not exactly imitate the words " Self-Washer," but used such words as a person not carefully weighing each word upon the two wrappers might easily mis- take for the words " Self -Washer." The defenclAate attempted to justify their action by saying that the representation of the sun shining was their trade mark. He contended that they had put the sun shining—the sun in splendour—to make it similar to the words Sunlight," so that those persons who had been accustomed to purchase plaintiff's soap, or had been accifstomed to have it described partly as "sunlight," when they saw the sun in splendour, coupled with the word S " Genuine Sun," would be led to suppose that it was the Sunlight Soap they knew so well, especially when the simi- larity of appearance was considered. Defendants did not say that because plaintiff's soap Suited the public, was good, and novel in its make they manufactured a soap in honest competition in order also to suit the public taste. They said they did not imitate the soap, and that the soap they were selling under the new form of matter was identically the same as they had sold for years. What object then in suddenly chang- ing and adopting the size, shape, make, and get-up of plaintiff's soap, if not to obtain the benefit of plaintiff's reputation. After a long diseutoien be- tween the counsel engaged in the case, his Lordship said that he could not advance it, seeing what the state of lists was, so as to try it before the Long Vacation, but if the defendants kept an account, then he would allow an application to advance it so as to be heard before Christmas. Mr. Macnaughten said that of course they would do that, but the order would be without prejudice. His Lordship said that undertaking might be given without prejudice to any question.

ST. HELENS COUNTY COURT. WEDNESDAY—Before Judge Collier. CLAIM AGAINST A CAB PROPRIETOIL—Abrahun Chirg- win, a painter and coachbuilder, St. Helens, brought an ac- tion for the recovery of £4 19a from William G. Dixon, cab proprietor, St. Helens. The defendant did not appear. —Mr. R. W. 11. Thomas, solicitor, who appeared for the plaintiff, stated that the amount named was the balance of an account, amounting to £26 198, for painting and repair- ing coaches and carriages belonging to the defendant. The bill for £26 19a had been rendered in due course and pay- ' ments were made from time to time, the total amounting to £22, leaving the balance, to recover which this action was brought.—Tbe Judge asked if the defendant ever admitted the amount alleged to be owing.—Plaintiff replied that he had an objection to it at first, and offared £l6 in settlement of it —His Honour made an order for the amount claimed, with costs. A WIDNES BUILDER'S TRANSACTIONS.—AD action to re- cover the sum of £29 68 7d, as the balance of an account front Thomas Sadler, a builder, at Widnes, was brought by T. D. Wainwright, a master plumber and glazier, at Liver- pool. Mr. H. L. Riley, solicitor, St. Helens, appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. T. Swift, barrisler, Liverpool, repre- sented the defendant —Mr. Riley said the amount of the claim was the balance of an account in respect to work done, amounting in value to several hundreds of pounds, in con- nection with property at Widnes. The defendant had set up a counter-claim of £ll 4s 4cl for work left undone, but particulars of that had only been received that morning.— Mr. Swift remarked that the counter-claim was really ad- mitted, and he did not anticipate any difficulty in that respect. —The plaintiff was then called. He said that be- tween 1877 and 1880 be did work for the defendant,amount- ing in value to £423 3s sd. lie had received in cash and !labour £393 Hs 10d, leaving the balance of £29 163 7d. He had seen the particulars of the counter-claim for the first time that morning, and he admitted the items with the exception of one of £1 108. He admitted it for the purpose of a settlement, but he did not know whether it was correct or not.—Mr. Swift said the claim was one for work done, and he thought the only question was bad the work been done. He held that the work bad not been completed, for which certain deductions included in the counter-claim had been made.—The Judge afterwards suggested an arrange- ment, and the parties left the court.—On their return, Mr. Swift said they had agreed to accept judgment for £8 6.3 4d without costs to either side.

father' i hoi;se.armed with a gun, ad demanded his share of his late father's property, and then shot his step-father— named linger—through the head. Rogers then jumped into a neighbouring river and was drowned. THE DYNAMITE OUTRAGES.—The Rome Secretary has, it is stated, ordered the relaxation of those special m ecautions which were taken immediately after the late dynamite ex- plosions, as there have been no outrages since the arrest of Cunningham and Burton. The special officers who were employed will be sent back to resume their ordinary duties in Ireland.

SHOCKING DEATH OF AN IRONFOTINDER.-011 Thursday morning, Mr. Thomas Sagar, ironfounder, Burnley, suc- cumbed to injuries received at his own works in Hamerton- street, on Wednesdiy. He was passing under the hoist when a mashing machine crate, weighing one cwt., fell upon him inflicting dreadful injuries to the head and other parts of the body. ACCIDENT TO A. CRICKET PARTY.—A brake, containing 20 young men, returning to &ahem Harbour from a cricket match on Saturday night, broke down in Sunderland, through the fracture of one of the wheels. All the occu- pants were thrown out, and several were badly out and bruised. Joseph Paxton being so badly injured that he had to be removed to the Sunderland Infirmary. THE DERBY.—The race for the Derby Stakes took place on Wednesday. The prize fell to Lord Hastings's Melton, the winner of the Two Thousand Guineas; Paradox being second. The French champion, Xaintrailles, did not suc- ceed in getting even among the " placed " horses, although ' many of the prophets had no doubt whatever of his ability to achieve that distinction, if even he did not absolutely win. THE IRONWORKERS' SPORTS, TELE WARRINGTON INFIRMAItY, AND Slit G. GNEENALL. Sir,—Tne ironworkers of oar town, with a zeal which does them great credit, have for some years past, very success- fully raised a considerable sum of money for the benefit of our infirmary. Every year, as the time for the sports draw nigh, circulars are sent round to the various leading men in the neighbourhood soliciting subscriptions to this worthy object. This year. as usual, these circulars were sent out, and amonget others one was sent to Sir Gilbert Greenell. In due course a reply 01,18 received from the ben. gentleman I to the effect that ha c mid not accede to the request con- tained in the circular as he was already a subscriber to the Tarmary, This was all very well and very proper, but a line& Wall in store for Wall, when, on the day of the sports we heard it announced that Sir eillyirt bad sent through Captain Reynolds the sum of five pounds. All that lam curious about is to know bow, and by whom, Sir Gilbert was persuaded to change his mind (?) in reference to Va.'s matter? lam glad the Infirmary is benefited to the ex- tent of another £5 of Sir Gilbert's money, but the gracious- ness of the gift was all spoilt by the preliminary refusal. Perhaps Captain Rimolds, who does a god deal of Sir Gilbert's fetching and carrying, can explain the matter.— Yours, atc., LYNX. PROTECTION NO REMEDY FOR BAD TRADE. Sir,—The present condition of the iron-producing dis- tricts of the Uoited States is gloomy in the extreme. In Pittsburg all the large iron and steel works are closed. Further west, in the Mehoning region of Ohio, and at Wheeling, in a part of Virginia which lies between the two states of Pennsylvania and 011ie, all the work in the mills has ceabed. There are somewhere about 100,000 men idle, a strike having been ordered by the Amalgamated Associa- tion of Iron and Steel Workers to prevent a reduction of 20 to 25 per cent in wages, as prooosed by the masters. The workmen were, it seems, willing to submit to A reduc- tion of 10 per cent, and a compromise might have been brought about if the conditions of trade had been more favourable. The emanation in business is said to be un- precedented. Manufacturers complain that for some time they have been losing mosey. The market is reported to be glutted, and the preduction has of late been largely going Into stock. A consderable fall has taken place, and as a natural consequeoce a :eduction of wages has become in- evitable, and the expgctation is, that the works in the dis- tricts named will be closed throughout the summer. This unhappy condition of things in America may be commended to the consideration of those in this country whose faith in Free Trade may have been somewhat shaken by the depressed cendition of sores of our industries. Scarcely any Am-rican industry has been more fully or carefully protected than the iron and steel trade, and at the present time there is none in a worse condition. If Pro- tection had a:1 the virtues which are generally claimed for t, it would at least enable A trade such as the one in ques- tion to get throng° bed times with moderate ease. This, however, is by no mane the experience of the iron manu- facturers and wo-kmen of the United States. Perhaps Mr. Lawrenson (to whom, as the embodiment of commercial wisdom, one naturally turns) caa throw tome light upon this grave matter.—Yours truly, U. ROBERTS.

div.head: IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE.
div.p: THE IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE.

S r,—l would deem it a great favour if you would give me a corner in your paper to reply to Mr. Clifford Dix's letter. I will promise Mr. Dix that this is my last reply t 3 him. I admire a great portion of Mr. Dix's letter, as I firmly be- lieve that it is his desire to do goud to all her Majesty's subjects at home and abroad, especially to old Ireland. The only thing he doubts is whether the majority of my country- men are of the same mind. I can venture to tell him that out of every 100 Irishmen asked about Home Rule there will be 94 for it. As regards the several questions Mr. Dix already asks for by the chairman it was put all right at the follow- ing meeting. Why did not Mr. Dix come to that meeting, and then he would have more correct knowledge before he rustles to the press. "I am anxious," says Mr. Dix, "that Irish residents in the British Isles shall receive permanent and lasting benefit." lam glad to hear it. It might be called a humourous or playful speech about Mr. .1. G. Big- I gar, M.P., or any of the Irish Parliamentary party, In Mr. Dix's simp'e opinion, but tot so with the Warrington Irish- men. As for three cheers for the Mandi—that is nothing to look at. If Mr. Dix will look at the past great wars fought by Englishmen, Irishmen, Scotchmen, and Welshmen, he will find that in all battles Irishmen did their duty and gave I ringing cheers for the British army. Mr. Dix took a sudden jump to Widnes. All respects are due to T. P. O'Connor, Eaq , M.P. for County Galway, from the Irish people all over the world for his straightfor- ward principles in and out of the House of Commons. The respected chairman of the Widnes meeting is one of whom the Irish people of Lancashire are proud for his firm stand In behalf of justice to oppressed Ireland. I don't think it is fair of Mr. Dix to hold Warrington Irishmen responsinle for words said by any body of men in any place. What if! asked him about a speech delivered some 25 years ago by the Right Hoc. John Bright, M.P., when be charged her Maj:sty's Government, after 50 years' ruling of Ireland, that there Were no good measures passed for Ireland but three, namely, Public Works, Workhouses, and Gaols ; and since that time there is scarcely any good bills passed. The Irish Church when disestablished did a little good, I admit. But the Land Act is a failure, because it only approaches landlords and farmers. There is no compelling landlords to build suitthle homes for the p-rer in the Bill, so it is no use, or any advance in their wages of any kind. Look at four millions of poor people, and no justice or protec- tion.

In &acing over Mr. Dix's letter, I find he did not lay down any good measures that should be done at once by the Government ; nothing practical in bis letter; nothing but personal attacks. Let Mr. Dix act like Messrs. Cowan, Storey. Thompson, Jesse Collings, Labouchere, and several other M.P.'s The above English members of Parliament deserve the respect of all the Irish race over the world for their aiding the Irish Parliamentary party in most measures for the good of the Irish people. Coming to Sister Clare's History of Ireland, I will tell Mr. Dix that there Is not the right ring in it. It is a little on one side. But Mr. Ogle in his time was an ornament to the Irish Parliament. If Mr. Dix would read McGees, Johneton's, Butler's, Dr. Gallaher's and several other his- tories of Ireland he might see some true and sad things in them. In the last census returns of the United States there is given a table showing the nationality of all those engaged In situations of gain and profit. Toe principal nationalities represented are the United States, Ireland, Germany, end Great Britain. Of native barn Americans seven millions are engazed in agricultural pursaits, three millions in pro. fessional life, one million in on:rim-3rue, two and a half mil- lions in manufactury, making in all a total of thirteen and a half mlliilDS of money-earning Americans. For the other three nationalities the numbers are at toll we :
I,elanl Germany G..eat, Britaio. Agriculture 140,307 291 722 104 314 Professions 415,854 218.837 79,983 Commsrce 133 518 152.481 54 493 Manufactures 284,474 338,110 225,730

T0ta1..,, 973,563 1,033,190 40,50 Tte et:apet feature in the above table Is the compara- tively small number of Irish devoted to agriculture in the States. Of Germans there are more than twice as many as English and Scotch, almost as many in farming. But the vast majority of the Irish seem from the above figures to have gone into the more lucrative callings of the profes- sions, commerce, and manufactures. In the professions the Irish are twice as numerous as the Germans, lye times as strong as the British, and in commerce and manufac- tures they are a highly respectable element. Most of those emigrating from this country are of courso acquainted with agriculture alone ; but the high intelligence and ready powers of their race enabl•them soon to pass up to higher positions and to acquire mechanical trades. The above modes and methods are much wanted in all parts of Ireland, and the British Government ought to bring into Parlia- ment each measures as the people want. Nit acts like the present ones, but peace and contentment with all her Majesty's subjects, and thus strengthen the empire. Sir. years ago, when Mr. Bright was on a health tour in the Highlands, he wrote in a hotel book— Glen Huila seems to me a nobler glen ; Here sheep and deer have not supplanted men. _

I have never forgotten these lines, and I oftea wished Mr. Bright would go to 11Am:1(1-and there see how glen after glen has had its human population supplanted. In his great disestablishment speech, made two years ago, he re- ferred to wrongs three hundred years old. Yes, ho was a , noble champion when he said none of the church clergy protested against the imprisonment of live thousand Quakers under Charles It. Surely every Irishman ought thank him for this. I doll's want Mr. Clifford Dix hence- forth to twit Irishmen by foolishly raking up p t-t wrongs as regards old rotten dvnasti-s each as Mix anetn's ani Cromv.mil's, Irish assassinations of bishops, and clergy, and peonle, unspeaabls crtielt'es by proc-ss of supposed law, d )wn to the latest exploit of the cro vbar brigade. Quaker wrongs of two hunlrel years ago are nothing in comparison to how Ireland has been ruled. The Irish people haves p,rfect right to d,inand their rights and liberties in a fair and practical manner, and the Irish National League Is the best society for Irishmen of all &glades and•opinions to bring before the British people their grisvances in a straight- forward manner. The meetings are public, and all are in- vited is come.—Yours, PHILIP O'BRIEN. 38, Naylor-street, Warrington, June Ist, 1885. [With this letter, we close the correspondesce on this sub- ject.—ED., Ex]

div.head: WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIA-
div.p: WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIA-
' TION. SPEECH BY MR. McMINNIES, M.P.

A meeting of the General Council of the Warring- ton Liberal Association, at which a large number of members were present, was held in the Assembly- room of the Liberal Club, Bewsey-street, on Thurs- day evening, to consider a resolution, of which due notice had been given. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. G. McMinmes, member for the borough, who was loudly cheered on entering ths room.; and amongst those also present were the Rev. R. Fil- cher, 8.A., Rev. J. Yonge, Messrs. C. Broadbent, Z. Armitage, J. Walker, A. Browne, C. S. Burgess, and F. Dixon, and H. Roberts (secretary). Before the commencement of the proceedings, Mr. H. Roberts read letters of regret from several gentlemen who ; were not able to be present, Mr. William Crosfleld wrote,. saying that he had received an invitation to the meeting, but had already engaged to take part in a conference of working-men who were under- taking a vigorous movement in connection with • their -Hospital Saturday. Mr. John Crosfleld had been away during the whole time that the meeting had been arranged for, or he would have been there. Mr. Frederick Monks was in London, and wished Mr. Roberts to apologise for his absence. Coun- cillor Fleming, who was also not able to be present, telegraphed to the effect that he was entirely in ac- cord with the proposed resolution, and Dr. Gomall wrote statingthat a somewhat serious illness would prevent him from attending, and added that he should with pleasure have supported the resolution 11 to be subnutted, because he had lost none of his .1 attachment to Liberalism—the foundation of all that was righteous in the government of the coun- try. There was not a Liberal in Warrington who had any sympathy with coercion, whether applied to the Irish nation, the Dissenters, or to the rest of the nation in the existence of an Established Church. That was Toryism, which, in his memory had always been allied with injustice, oppression, and , untruthfulness. It having been explained that the . meeting had been convened at the request of a , member who wished to submit a resolution, '

Mr. Thomas Flood rose to propose "That this meeting desires to express its confidence in and ap- proval of the policy of her Majesty's Government; thanks them for their promised Irish reforms— especially for the intended amendment of the Land Purchase Clauses—and suggests that the present condition of Ireland does not justify the proposed infliction of further coercive legislation." Refemng to England and Russia, he said tlytt one of the grandest achievements of a noble life had resulted in saving the country from a calamitous war, and a statesnian who had averted such a catastrophe deserved the praise of the civilised world. They hailed, he said, speaking to the latter part of the resolution, an ap- proach to land reform in Ireland, which had always been opposed by the Tories, for they knew the de- gradation in which the Irish peasant had existed for the last 30 or 40 years. He spoke effectively on thb Irish question, and concluded by saying that they must use all legitimate means to show our brethren across the sea that they were anxious to take them by the hand. (Applause.) Mr. Michael Chambers seconded the resolution. Coeition, in his opinion, had been a blow to Ire- land that had driven its best blood abroad. (Ap- plause.) Messrs. H. Whitham, H. Roberts, W. Stirrup, Barnes, and Weir made short speeches on the reso- lution. Mr. McMinnies, M.P., who was received with loud applause, said: It has been my custom since I went to Parliament to make some remarks in Mid-Session, not to a general meeting of the party, , but at any rate to a representative meeting of the party such as we have here to-night—(hear, hear)— and it is my wish to take this opportunity to con- tinue that practice, and of making some remarks to ! you to-night in reference to politics generally, and to' the Irish question in particular. (Hear, hear.) But in order that I may be quite in connection with my position as chairman, which obliges me to keep order—you know that if a chairman is not orderly he is not anything—in order that I may be in order I shall make the remarks that I have to put before you on the lines of the resolution .3vhich has been moved by Mr. Flood. (Hear.) You will observe that the resolution points in three directions. In the first place it expresses its approval of her Majesty's Government as regards their peaceable foreign policy, and their proposed introduction of remedial measures during this session in reference to Ireland, and it suggests, or urges, if our friend likes it better, that the condition of Ireland does not at the present time justify the renewal of the Crimes Act. (Hear, hear.) Well, as regards our foreign policy, I suppose that there is no man, whatever his political opinions may be, who is entirely satisfied with the position of this country In reference to foreign affairs—(hear)--but I do not believe that Government is to blare for what is going on in various parts of the world. I be- lieve that most of their complications and difficul- ties have been inherited from their predecessors —(applause)---and' I think that a good deal of the remaining complications and difficulties hs.-ve been such as no Government could avoid meeting when they arose, and dealing with. (Hear, hear.) I think that no small portion of our difficulties in Egypt arose from the erratic conduct of that un- fortunate and misguided man—Gordon. Well, now, the Tory party have a great deal to say about the present Government in reference to their foreign policy, and there is one word that they use very frequently—vacillation. I do not know what they mean by vacillation exactly, and I do not suppose they know either, but it appears to me • that the Government are to blame because they do not go ta war with every government in Europe, unless they have their own way in every matter that they deal with. (Hear, hear.) You will observe that vacillation is a long word and a high sounding word. It reminds me very much of the story told of a pious old lady who said that she could not be sufficiently thankful to God for that comforting word Mesopotamia. (Laughter.) The Tories claim to be the patriotic party i in this country, but do you see raiich patriotism in the tone of their speeches fold writings when at the present time they are declaring to this country and to the whole world—that the Government of this coun- try is flouted and thwarted, and disliked and hated, throughout the world—(hear, hear)—and that if any nation in Europe wants anything it has only to bully the English Government and they will get it? Do you think that that is patriotism? Sup- posing that they are right in saying that the Govern- ment is what they say—weak, impotent, disliked, thwarted—what must that Government be that the

-- people of this country so dread that they will put , up with the incapacity of the present Government . rather than see it in power? (Applause.) If Lord Granville and Mr. Gladstone are so incapable, what ' must Lord Salisbury and Lord Randolph Churchill be? (Applause.) The country will submit to the so-called incapacity of the present Government rather than face that unknown dread of a Tory policy. (Hear, hear.) Well, now, the Government have done something. We at any rate see an end to our difficulties in Egypt, and they have got us out of the difficulty with Russia. (Hear, hear.) If the Tory party had been in power, and under Lord Salisbury and Lord Randolph Churchill, I believe we should have been at war at the present time : with at least two great nations in Europe. The present Government have preserved us from that. (Applause.) I believe that the Tory party want war. (Hear, hear.) I believe that they long for. it. (Applause.) The appearance of the Tory counten- ance in the House of Commons when Mr. Gladstone

div.head: TEST NEWS.
div.p: LA TEST NEWS.

The London Gazette contains a notification of the British protectorate of the Niger districts. The Princess Louse arrived in London on Friday morn- ing from Balmoral. She was met at the station by the Marquis of Lorne. Sir Julius Benedict, the well•known musical composer and conductor, died at his London residence on Friday morning. He was in his filet var. The betting prosecutions at Manchester concluded yes- terday. In the Falmouth Club case two men were fined £4O, and five others £25 each ; and four bookmakers of the City Club £25 each. . . . . . . .

young man employad in a brick field at Shepherds Rush, London, on Thursday, was rendered unconscious by the heat. He was taken home in a cart, and aftet wards died from sunstroke. San DEATH raom DnowstNa.—At Winsford, on Thurs- day evening, Richard Goulding, a young man in the em- ploy of Messrs. Geo. Deakin, Winsford, fell into the Weaver and was drowned, though aid was immediately rendered. IMPRISONED IN A SEWER,-00 Friday morning a number of men were tunnelling in Stoke Newington, London, when the ground fell in burying two of the men. One was killed, sod it is feared the other will be drowned before he can be reached.

TRIAL FOR MURDER.—At the Dublin Commission Court on Friday, Frederick Keenan, army reserve man, was Put I on his trial on a charge of having. is April last, murdered Eliza Keenan, an unfortunate, With whom he cohabited. He pleaded not guilty. Tun ADAMS V. COLERIDGE CASE.—The hearing of Mr. Adam's appeal in his actien against the Hon. Bernard Cole- ridge was resumed on Friday, before the Master of the Rolls and Lords Justices Baggalay and Lindley. The Attorney General continued his argument for the defendant, contend- ing that in privileged "communications it was unnecessary to show a statement was true to defend a p.rson making it from the charge of libel. He maintained there was no proof of malice in the letter complained of, defendant only seeking his sister's advantage. Mr. Charles followed on the same side. Mr. Adams having replied, their Lordships, after , a brief private deliberation, postponed judgment until Monday.
DOUBLE MURDER BY-A MOTHER AND ATTEMPTED SUICIDE.

About noon on Friday information was received at the Rusholme Police Station that a woman had murdered her two children, aged three and live respectively, and then at- tempted to commit suicide by drowning'. Inspector Smith went at once to 54, Fern Leaf-street, Moss Side, and found the two children lying on a bed in one of the bedrooms naked and quite dead, apparently from drowning. Upon the body of one of the children there was a piece of paper containing some almost illegible writing. What portions of it that could be made out ran as follows : " Dear Papa,—l could not stand it any longer . . . to you. I do not think they are del I,for they . . We shall never meet in heaven. I could net help it. I had a good husband." The Inspector took Mrs. Hibbert to the Busholme Police Station, where she now lie.. The unfor- tunate woman is. it appears, the wife of Thomas Hibbert, joiner and builder. About twelve months ago Mrs. Hibbert gave birth to a child. She fell ill, and finally became in- sane. She was removed to the Parktield Asylum, near Macclesfield, of which institution she was an inmate up till the 3rd of this month. Mr. Hibbert left the house about eight o'clock in order to proceed to his work, but prior to his doing so he gave strict orders to Ids servant to keep an eye upon her mistress's movements. About nine o'clock Mrs. Ilibbert told the servant to call the children from playing in the front garden. Mrs. Hibbert took bold of the children and took them !upstairs with her. She came down shortly afterwards and sent the servant for a bolts of soda saying that she felt unwell. On the servant's return with the soda water, she asked her mistress what had become of the children. Becoming alarmed, she procured a neighbour, and on reaching the house they heard a splashing in the bathroom. They proceeded thither, and found Mrs. Hiboert in the bath. They asked her where the children were and Mrs. Hibbert replied, "I have drowned them. I don't think they are dead, as they are quite warm." She took them into a bedroom where the two children were found lying quite naked on the bed, and although the bodies were warm they were perfectly dead. Mrs. Hibbert also told them she had been trying to drown herself in the bath for the last half hour.

THE RUSSIAN NAVY. - BERLIN, FRlDAY.—lntelligence from St. Petersburg an. nounces that the Russian Admiralty has issued an order directing that all Russian war vessels are to be kept fully equippe I for active service. The Baltic Fleet commenced a aeries of naval manoeuvre/a to-day. AFFAIRS IN MADAGASCAR. The Times second edition contains the following telegram dated Durban, Friday :—lt is reported from Madagascar that the Prime Minister is dead, having been a victim of tee revolutionary feeling prevalent at Antananarivo ; also that the peace party is now in power. THE EARTHQUAKE IN CASHMERE. SIMLL FRIDAY.—A further report from the British Resi- dence in Cashentie, states that in the earthquake shocks at Srinugar, on the 31et nit, and let inst., 87 people were killed and 100 injered. There is also some loss of life in the neighbouring villages, but to what extent is not yet known.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.
The House met at 4 o'clock.

NISCELLANEOITS.—EarI Cairns took his seat in succession to his father. A motion by Lord Greville for a Select Corn- mittee to consider the working of the Friendly Societies Act respecting the registration of new societies was negatived.— E GRANVILLB, replying to Earl Stanhope, said he was unable to give any information respecting the proceedings of the Suez Canal Committee Mission till after the conclu- sion of their sittings, The basis of arrangement was that stated in the Circular of January, 1.853.—The East India (Uuclaimed Stocks) Bill passed the second reading.—The House soon afterwards adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four o'clock.

NOTICES.—Mr. Arnold gave notice that he should put a question as to the conversation said to have taken place between Sir P. Lumsden and reporters of various news- papers.—Mr. Chaplin gave notice that on that day month he should call attention to the continued depress:on in agri- culture, and move a resolution. BODGET PROPOSALS.— rile CHANCELLOR Of the EX- CHEQUER said nine midions out of the Vote of Credit had been expended. The altered circumstances would enable him to make a change in his Budget proposals. There would be no alteration in the income tax or direct taxation but instead of an increased duty of 23 per gallon on Brltiah and foreign spirits, they proposed the increased duty should be is, and a resolution would be moved that night in order that the alteration might take effect immediately. As re- girds the increased beer duty, they did not propose any change, but the additional duty would silly exist up to 31st May next. They did not propose any alteration of the wine duties, and the resolution on that subject would re- main unchanged. In reply to a question, the Chancellor of the Exchequer said those who bad paid increased duty would not receive it back.

ENGLAND AND RIISSIA.—Mr. GLADSTONE, replyi-g to a question, said that Russia had agreed that the Afghan fron- tier question should be referred to the arbitration of an illustrious person, but the terms of agreena,nt had not been finally decided. On neither side had the illustrious person baen communicated with. Mr. Gladstone, replying to Mr. Chaplin, said, regarding the statement appearing in the Times as to communications made by Sir P. Lumaden, that nothing to the rffect stated had reached the Government.— Lord HARTINGTON, replying to Co:onel Digby, said the stay of the Guards at Alexandria would not be long; he could not then state the exact period of their departure. ORDER OF BUSINESS.—Mr. GLADSTONE stated that the Customs and Inland Revenue Bill would be taken on Mon- day, and a bill to replace the Crimes Act would be intro- duced on Thursday. •

SrPPLY.—On the motion to go into Committee of Supply Mr. T. D. SULLIVAN called attention to the means by which convictions for a conspiracy to murder were obtained against certain prisoners from the neighbourhood of Barba- voile, county of Westmeath. He said he had made search- ing inquiry into the whole of the circumstances attendirg the conviction, and he believed the parties found guilty to be entirely innocent. lie urged the Government to allow 'the whole matter to be re-investigated by an impartial per- son—The ATTORNEY•GENERAL for IRELAND Caid the !nor- I der was committed on Sun.tay, April ren, 1882, as tha lady was returning from church in a close carriage, and eleven men were charged with conspiracy to Murder, because no human eye saw the murder committed. As the various witnesses were corroborated, and there would be no safety in ci 'veinal trial if the verdict of the jury was set aside After some discussion, Mr. WARTON intimated that there were not forty members present. The !louse was counted.; only 36 were present, and the House adjourned at 8 Lintel Monday.
